story:
Luca had not expected the robotics track at Camp Winnowick to contain homework, and he told anyone who would listen that signing up for Java in July was like volunteering to convalesce at a dentist's office. His counselor, Priya, had only smiled and said the laptop lab had air conditioning, which in a camp where mosquitos were practically endemic counted as a luxury resort.

The project was simple on paper: build a class called SongList with private fields and getter methods, then test it. Priya handed out cards with the requirements and then sat in the corner, refusing to answer questions, which made her, in Dara's words, "an autocrat of the silent variety." Dara was the girl at the terminal next to Luca's, twelve years old, allergic to being wrong, and the fastest typist in the cabin.

"Private means private," Dara announced on the second morning, scrolling through Luca's screen without asking. "Your songs are hidden. Nobody can touch them. It's like a vault."

"A vault with a door you built," Luca said, because he had learned the getter methods by then, the little public methods named getSongs and getSize that handed the vault's contents out to anyone who asked. His test class called getSongs forty times an hour. Everything worked. He had a list of eleven campfire songs stored in his SongList object, and the test printed them all, and he felt the specific smugness of a sixteen-year-old whose code compiles on the first try.

Then came the twist, though at first it looked like a catastrophe. On Thursday afternoon Dara borrowed his SongList class for her own project, a game where a grumpy camp director confiscates songs from campers. Her Confiscator class called getSongs, and somewhere in her code she called clear on whatever came back, the way you'd empty a bin. When Luca reopened his test afterward, his SongList, his private, protected, carefully encapsulated SongList, printed zero songs. Eleven songs, gone. He stared at the empty output like a man who'd locked his house and come home to find the furniture on the lawn.

"That's your bug," Dara said, when he accused her. "Your vault. Your door."

"It's private," Luca said. "I typed the word private. It's right there."

They fought about it for a full ten minutes, politely at first and then with escalating accusations involving each other's mothers and formatting habits, until Priya finally drifted over, looked at two lines of code, and said only, "Interesting. What did getSongs actually hand back?" Then she wandered away again, which was her version of teaching.

Luca sat with the question. He wrote a tiny experiment: he made a SongList, called getSongs, added a song to the thing it returned, and printed the list again. The original SongList had grown by one. He ran it twice more, then leaned back so fast his chair squeaked. The getter wasn't handing out a copy of his list. It was handing out the list itself, the actual object, the same one living behind the word private. His vault door opened directly onto the vault. Dara's Confiscator hadn't broken in; he'd handed it the key and called it hospitality.

"So it's not really private at all," he said out loud, to no one.

"It's private the way my diary is private when I read it aloud at dinner," Dara said, which was generous of her, since it was her code that had emptied his list.

Luca rewrote the getter that evening while the rest of the cabin was at the campfire. Instead of returning the list directly, he built a new list in the getter, put the same songs into it, and returned that. Now Dara's Confiscator could clear its little heart out; it would only be emptying the copy. He tested it by letting her game confiscate everything twice, and his original still printed all eleven songs, stubborn as a raccoon in a trash can. He made her run her whole project again, and when the final line of his test printed "11 songs remaining," he stood up and did a small, shameful victory dance that Dara filmed.

There was a piece he still couldn't quite settle, and he was honest about it at the talent show the next night, when Priya asked what he'd learned. "Copies are safer," he said, holding the microphone like a man accepting an award. "But if my list were huge, I'd be copying it every time somebody asked to look. I don't know which is worse yet." He shrugged. "Ask me in September."

"What I learned," Dara called from the third row, "is that Luca's vault had a revolving door."

"It had a door that led directly to the vault," Luca corrected. "There's a difference, and it cost me eleven songs." He sat down to applause from people who had no idea what he was talking about, and Priya, in the back, raised her cup of bug juice to him.

story:
The party was in Dara's backyard, which meant paper lanterns on the fence and a playlist someone's older brother had codified into three hours of songs no one admitted to loving. Brooklyn arrived holding a Tupperware of brownies and a laptop bag, because the robotics notebook was due at midnight and the presentation was Monday, and she had promised herself she would not leave Dara's without telling Marcus what she actually thought about his code.

The trouble had started Tuesday, when Marcus had pushed his motor-control loop to the shared repository and Brooklyn had found, within four minutes, a sign error that would send the arm smashing downward instead of lifting. She had said nothing. She had said nothing on Wednesday too, and on Thursday, when Priya asked whether anyone had checked Marcus's section, Brooklyn had looked at the table and said it looked fine. That was the word she kept returning to, fine, sitting in her mouth like a coin.

"Brooklyn, you're at a party," Priya said now, handing her a cup of punch. "Why do you have the laptop out?"

"Because at midnight the notebook locks. And somebody has to tell him his loop is wrong before it's in the submitted version forever."

"So tell him."

"It's not that simple."

"It's exactly that simple. You've made a whole philosophy out of it."

Brooklyn had, a little. Her mother's approach, inherited from a family that praised everything, held that kindness meant never letting someone feel small. Her physics teacher's approach, which she distrusted and admired, held that precision was a form of respect and feelings could be sorted later. Somewhere between the two was a position she couldn't quite reach, and midnight was coming.

Marcus was by the fence, teaching a sophomore how to fold a napkin into a swan, badly, with enormous confidence. She watched him fail three times, laughing each time, and thought about how easily he shrugged off napkin mistakes and how she had no idea what he did with code mistakes, because in four months of building the robot together, no one on the team had ever admitted one out loud. Not once. It was a strange thing to notice at a birthday party, with lantern light on the grass and someone's terrible karaoke starting up by the garage, a small cold foreboding under the cake and the noise.

She found Priya again by the drink table. "That article you sent me. The team research one."

"Edmondson? You read it?"

"Twice. She called it psychological safety," Brooklyn said. "In 1999. A team's shared belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake."

"And we don't have it."

"Marcus broke a servo in October and blamed the manufacturer. Priya, I hid a wiring error for two days in November. Nobody in our group has ever said the words 'I messed up' to anybody else."

"So you're going to break the streak."

"I'm going to try not to break Marcus instead." She took a brownie from her own Tupperware for courage, which was a canny move in the sense that it bought her ninety seconds of chewing instead of talking.

She caught Marcus alone by the beanbag toss. "Can I show you something before midnight? It's about the loop."

He set down his beanbags. "Is it bad?"

"It's one line. Line two-forty. You're subtracting where you meant to add, so the arm goes down when the sensor says up. I tested it in simulation, that's how I found it, not by staring at your code being smarter than you."

He looked at the grass. "Why didn't you say something Tuesday?"

Because she had been afraid of this exact face. "I was a coward," she said. "I told myself I was being nice. But nice would have been telling you in time to fix it calmly instead of at a birthday party at eleven p.m."

He laughed at that, a real one, surprised out of him. "Okay. Line two-forty." They sat on the picnic table with the laptop between them, and he fixed it in one minute, and then he said, quietly, "I broke that servo myself, you know. Dropped it on the shop floor."

"I hid a wiring error in November," she said. "For two days."

"You're kidding."

"Priya knows. Now you do. It's apparently that kind of night." The lanterns buzzed faintly overhead; somewhere behind them, the karaoke had reached a high note it should not have attempted, and they both winced and laughed.

At 11:58 they committed the notebook, and Marcus raised his cup of punch and said, "To fine," and Brooklyn understood that he had heard her use the word on Thursday and had known, even then, that it was a lie. They didn't resolve anything larger. The team would have to learn this again on Monday, and probably after that, and Priya was already yelling at them to come inside for cake before someone ate the corner piece with the frosting rose.

Brooklyn closed the laptop and followed him toward the lights, leaving the last brownie on the picnic table for whoever found it.

story:
The laminated card had eleven bullet points on it, and James had read it so many times that the words had started to feel like weather, something that happened to him rather than something he said. He was nineteen days into his job as a junior counselor at Camp Wanoka, and the health director, Rhonda, had decided that the oldest campers, the fifteen and sixteen year olds, would get a session on consent, contraception and testing, and that James would lead it. He was eighteen. He had learned what a dental dam was on Tuesday.

His first attempt had gone badly in a way he was still turning over. He had stood in front of seventeen teenagers in the craft shed, recited the bullet points in the flat elocution of a boy reading a fire safety poster, and watched their faces close one by one, like shop doors at the end of a street. A girl named Priya had finally said, "Do you actually know anything, or did they just hand you a card?" He had said the honest thing, which was the card, and she had laughed, and the laugh had been worse than the silence.

He practiced after that in the empty boathouse, saying it out loud to the lake. Consent is ongoing and it can be withdrawn. Contraception reduces risk but nothing eliminates it except abstinence, and if you say abstinence like a threat nobody hears the rest. He found that if he admitted what he did not know, the sentences opened up instead of closing. This felt like a discovery he could not quite put into words, so he kept saying it to the lake.

The problem came to find him on Thursday, at the picnic table behind the infirmary, where a camper named Dominic was pretending to rearrange a first aid kit that Rhonda had already arranged. Dominic was sixteen and phlegmatic by nature, slow to alarm, which made it stranger that his hands would not stay still. He asked whether the clinic in town would call his mother. He said a girl from his school, in June, and he did not finish the sentence. He said, "They'd need a form. Everything needs a form. My mom signed a form so I could go on the sail trip."

James did not know. This was the part he would later understand as the real beginning, the moment when the card ran out. He walked Dominic to the infirmary and stood beside him while Rhonda called the county clinic, and he listened to her side of the conversation, which was mostly nodding sounds. When she hung up she said it plainly, without ceremony: all fifty states and Washington, DC, allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age. She said Dominic was over any minimum age here, and that no one at the clinic would call his mother, and that she would drive him herself on her supply run Friday morning.

Dominic looked at James then, not at Rhonda, and James understood that Dominic needed to hear it twice, from someone closer to his own age, from someone who would be there Saturday and Sunday and the week after. So James said it again, all fifty states and DC, no parent's permission, some states set a minimum age, and heard the sentence become true in his own mouth. They arranged to meet at the dock at eight. Dominic shook his hand, formally, like a man closing a deal, and went to find his bunkmates.

The session on Saturday went better than the one in the craft shed, though not because James had become smooth. He told the seventeen campers about Dominic, with permission, with the details sanded off, and he told them the law the way Rhonda had said it, and he asked them what they thought consent actually required of a person, and he let the silence sit until Priya said, "Asking, and meaning it when they answer," which was better than any bullet point. The campers argued about whether sixteen was old enough for any of it, and a boy named Felix said his older brother had gotten tested and it had taken twenty minutes, and James realized he was barely talking anymore, and that this was the job.

Friday morning, though, the dock at eight had been empty. Dominic had not come. Rhonda made the supply run alone, and when James found him later, shooting baskets on the cracked court behind the mess hall, Dominic said his mother had surprised him with a visit day, and she was here, right now, in the parking lot, unloading a cooler of sandwiches, and he could not do it this week. He would do it after camp, he said. He said it looking at the ball in his hands.

James wanted to argue and found he could not, because the law gave Dominic the right to decide, and deciding included deciding not yet, and that was the same principle he had been teaching, turned around and pointed at him like a joke with no punchline. He said he would sit with Dominic on the bus home if Dominic wanted, and talk about which clinic was near his house. Dominic said okay, and banked the ball off the backboard, and it rolled to the fence and stopped there in the long grass, and neither of them went to get it.

story:
John stood at the bathroom mirror with his phone balanced against the soap dish, rehearsing. He had volunteered, somewhat against his own expectations, to run the consent workshop for the freshman health seminar, and tomorrow afternoon three separate classrooms of younger students would look at him while he tried to explain things that a nurse practitioner had explained to him only two weeks ago.

The bathroom was the only room in the house with a lock his mother respected, so it had become his rehearsal space. He pressed record on the voice memo app, faced himself, and said, "Consent is a yes you can say out loud, and it has to be a yes you could change." He stopped. The sentence sounded like a poster. He tried again. "If someone is asleep, they can't say yes. If someone says yes because they're scared of what happens if they say no, that isn't a yes either." Better, but his voice in the recording was flat, and he wondered whether the flatness came from the bathroom's acoustics or from him.

His younger sister, Ruth, knocked twice and said through the door that she needed to pee. He told her to wait four minutes. She said, "You've been in there since dinner," and then, quieter, "Is this about that clinic thing?"

He opened the door. Ruth stood in the hallway in her soccer shorts, and behind her, holding two mugs of tea as though they portended some long and terrible conversation, was his mother. "Nurse Alvarez called back," his mother said. "About the peer health program. She wants to know if you'd also cover the testing part tomorrow."

John let them both into the bathroom, which was absurd, but it was where his notes were: the clinic pamphlet on the edge of the tub, the index card with the phone number, the printed schedule of drop-in hours. He sat on the closed toilet lid. Ruth leaned against the sink. His mother remained standing, truculent in the way she got when she felt she'd been maneuvered.

"You went to the clinic yourself?" Ruth said. "You said you were at Devin's."

"I was at the clinic," John said. "Then I was at Devin's. I got tested." He said it plainly because saying it plainly was the whole thing he was trying to learn. "I felt completely fine, so I figured I didn't need to, and then at the appointment the nurse told me that chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so a test is the only reliable way to know whether you have one. Feeling fine doesn't prove anything. That's actually the one fact I'm sure I'll get right tomorrow."

Ruth pulled the pamphlet from the tub and read it. "So you could have something right now and not know it."

"That's what testing is for," he said. "It's not a punishment. It's fifteen minutes and it's free, and the nurse was nicer to me than my dentist ever is."

His mother set the mugs down on the shelf where his father's shaving foam used to live. "You didn't tell us you were going."

"Because it would have become a whole family summit," John said. "Like this one." He picked up the index card and turned it over. On the back he had written his outline for the workshop, the sequence he'd built out of the nurse's practical heuristic: name the thing, describe the action, give the next concrete step. Say what consent is. Say what contraception does and where to get it. Say where the clinic is, that it's confidential, that you don't need a parent, and that the test is the only way to know, because the infections usually show nothing.

"You're doing this tomorrow," his mother said. It was half a question.

"Three periods," John said. "Ms. Okafor signed off."

Ruth handed back the pamphlet. "You're going to stand in front of freshmen and talk about this. You, who threw up before the eighth grade spelling bee."

"I know," John said.

"What if someone asks you something you can't answer?"

He looked at the card. There were gaps in it, real ones. He could explain consent as a principle and still not know what to say to a kid whose girlfriend said yes out of habit, or whose parents had taught him something entirely different, or who believed, with total certainty, that a person who looked healthy was healthy. He could give the clinic's address and still not know how a sixteen-year-old without a car was supposed to get there on a Tuesday afternoon. "Then I'll say I don't know," he said. "And I'll write it down and ask Nurse Alvarez."

His mother finally sat on the edge of the tub. "I'm not angry," she said. "I was going to be angry. I had it prepared. But you went, and you came back, and now you're teaching it, and I don't know what to do with a son who does the sensible thing without telling me."

"Be annoyed quietly," Ruth said. "I need to pee."

After she left, his mother stood, kissed the top of his head, which she hadn't done since he was eleven, and carried both untouched mugs of tea back down the hall. John locked the door, looked at himself in the mirror, and started recording again. "Consent is a yes you can say out loud," he told his reflection, "and it has to be a yes you could change. And if you've had sex, get tested, because feeling fine isn't proof of anything. The clinic's on Fenwick Street. Drop-in hours are Tuesdays." He stopped the recording and played it back. His voice sounded less flat than before. He pressed record and started over.

story:
The camp's health lodge smelled like sunscreen and grape bubblegum, and Rachel had volunteered there mostly to escape the dining hall dishes, so it was a kind of cosmic joke that the first thing Nurse Padma taught her was a machine. "Systolic over diastolic," Padma said, fastening the cuff around a counselor's tanned arm. "Top number, bottom number. Top is when the heart pushes, bottom is when it rests." Rachel wrote it on her forearm in pen, which Padma pretended not to notice.

The want came later, on a Tuesday, when Joanie from Cabin 4 tripped over a canoe and opened her knee. While Padma stitched, she asked Rachel to take Joanie's pressure, and the little screen blinked up 148 over 92, numbers that meant nothing to Rachel until Padma's eyebrows did something complicated. "That's high," Padma said. "For a kid." Rachel felt her stomach drop as if she'd been the one to bleed.

Joanie, being Joanie, was delighted to have a medical condition. She narrated it to the whole cabin that night, lying on her bunk with her knee elevated on a pillow like a queen's foot. "My blood pressure," she announced, "is famous." The other girls were less impressed, because Joanie also claimed to be allergic to mosquitoes, thunder, and the crepuscular hour between dinner and campfire, which she said made her "spiritually itchy." Rachel liked her anyway. Joanie was honest in a way that had no filter, an idiosyncrasy that made her terrible at cards and good at friendship.

Rachel, meanwhile, had spent the evening doing arithmetic she barely understood. If high pressure meant something bad, and Joanie had it, then something bad was happening, and Rachel had watched the numbers happen without stopping them. She found Padma by the supply shelf, restocking gauze. "Is Joanie sick?" she asked. "Like, actually?"

Padma didn't answer right away, which Rachel had learned meant the answer was a question. "What do you think happens to your body when you're nervous?" Rachel considered this. She thought of the paddling test she'd failed in June, how her hands had shaken so badly the paddle knocked her own hat off, twice, in front of everyone. "Everything gets loud," she said. "Fast. Like the heart's sprinting." Padma snapped the gauze box shut. "Take her pressure tomorrow morning," she said. "Before she's awake enough to perform for anyone."

So at seven the next morning, Rachel sat on the edge of Joanie's bunk with the cuff and the machine and a sense of mission she usually reserved for capturing the flag. Joanie, hair flat on one side, stuck out her arm without opening her eyes. The machine hummed, tightened, and released. 118 over 74. Rachel took it twice more because she didn't believe herself. Both times, normal.

She carried the numbers to the lodge like a relay baton. "Yesterday it was 148 over 92," she said, "in here, when she was bleeding and scared. This morning it's normal. So the machine isn't wrong. Something about the moment is." Padma smiled in the small way that meant Rachel had arrived somewhere on her own. "There's a name for it," Padma said. "White coat hypertension." She was already unscrewing a pen. "When it reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home. It's why we sometimes send people home with a cuff, or have them wear a monitor that checks all day, before anyone decides anything."

Rachel practiced saying it out loud on the walk to the lake, enjoying the weight of it. White coat hypertension. She imagined the blood pressure machine as a shy animal that only got startled around doctors, which was not the mechanism, she was fairly sure, but which made her laugh anyway. She tried explaining it to her co-CIT Marcus, who was mopping the boathouse. "So the number is true and also a lie," Marcus said, wringing the mop. "That's the most medical thing I've ever heard." "It's true in the moment," Rachel said. "It's just not the whole truth. You'd have to see her on an ordinary day to know her ordinary number."

That was the part she turned over for the rest of the week, because it seemed bigger than blood. A single reading, a single bad afternoon, a single failed paddling test: none of them told you what a person was, only what a person was right then. She wasn't sure how far the idea stretched, and she liked not being sure. On Friday she cuffed Joanie one last time by the campfire, partly for science and mostly for show. "Normal," Rachel reported. Joanie sighed, deeply disappointed. "So I'm not dying." "You're not dying." "Then at least tell me I'm allergic to the blood pressure machine," Joanie said, and held out her arm again.

story:
Gabrielle had been dreading the parallel parking more than the examiners, more than the roundabouts, more than anything on the syllabus, and so it was parallel parking she practised first, in her grandmother's gravel drive, between two plastic bins dragged out of the garage to stand in for parked cars. Her grandmother sat on the garden wall with a flask of tea, calling distances the way a coxswain calls a stroke. "More lock," she said. "No, more than that." Gabrielle turned the wheel and felt the nearside wheel kiss the kerb with a sound like a struck match.

She stopped the engine and put her forehead on the rim of the wheel. "That's it, isn't it. If I touch the kerb in the test, I've failed."

"Who told you that?"

"Everyone. It's all over the forums. Touch the kerb and you're done."

Her grandmother poured a second cup and said nothing, which was not her usual mode. She was a woman who gesticulated when she described so much as a supermarket queue, so the stillness meant something. "Look it up," she said at last. "Properly, not on a forum."

Gabrielle found the answer that evening at the kitchen table, her phone propped against the sugar bowl while her grandmother sliced plums for a crumble. On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passed with no more than fifteen driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults. She read it twice, then a third time, because the words refused to arrange themselves into the doom she'd been carrying around. "Fifteen," she said aloud. "You're allowed fifteen faults." Touching the kerb gently, according to a footnote in some official guidance she found afterwards, could count as one fault, a driving fault, the minor kind, and she still had fourteen left in the bank. The vast superstructure of terror she'd built on one grazed wheel was, apparently, a tower built on air. There were, of course, the other kinds, the serious and dangerous faults, each one fatal to the result on its own, and she could not quite see the border between a fault that was minor and a fault that was serious, and that unseen border unsettled her more than the number soothed her.

"So it's not one strike and out," her grandmother said, laying plums in a fan.

"It's fifteen strikes and out. And then some strikes count as the whole game."

Her grandmother laughed, a short bark that startled the cat. "That's very British. Generous and merciless at the same time."

The next problem was the merge, and it could not be solved in a gravel drive between two bins. The nearest motorway was forty minutes away, and for the first two of those forty minutes Gabrielle's grandmother rode with her hands folded in her lap, silent as a nun, before observing that silence in a passenger was not in any way calming and that Gabrielle's shoulders had risen nearly to her ears. They stopped at a lay-by and swapped the radio to a station neither of them liked, because it turned out that familiar music made her grandmother want to conduct, and conducting involved gesticulation, and a gesticulating passenger at seventy miles an hour was its own category of dangerous fault. The subterfuge with the radio worked: her grandmother settled, Gabrielle's shoulders descended, and at the next junction they watched a lorry bear down while a space opened beside it like a decision being made for her. She pressed the accelerator, slotted in, and heard her grandmother exhale a word she pretended not to hear.

They drove to the coast and back. On the way home, in the last light, they argued gently about the test itself, or rather about what it was for. Gabrielle had begun to think of the fifteen faults as a kind of grace, a system that assumed learners would err and still deserved to drive; her grandmother thought it assumed nothing so generous, only that examiners needed a scale and errors needed counting. "It's not forgiveness, love, it's arithmetic," she said. Gabrielle wasn't sure she agreed, and said so, and neither of them conceded, and somehow the disagreement was the pleasantest part of the whole day. She held both ideas in her hands the way she'd learned to hold the wheel at ten and two, not choosing yet.

On the morning of the test she parked between the examiner's cones without touching anything at all, not the kerb, not the bins of her imagination, nothing, and she used perhaps two of her fifteen faults on the roundabout near the industrial estate, and the examiner, a dry man with a clipboard, told her at the end that she had passed. She drove home alone, legally, for the first time, turned into her grandmother's road with the windows down, and executed, out of pure celebration, the most beautiful parallel park of her life in front of the garden wall. The nearside wheel kissed the kerb with a sound like a struck match.

Her grandmother, watching from the window, raised her flask in a slow salute. "Fault number one," she called through the glass.

story:
Savannah had circled the block twice before she let herself stop behind the silver sedan on Milberry Street, four car lengths of open curb beside it, the bank's brass doors waiting half a block down. Her road test was in six days. Her instructor, a stoic man named Ruiz who had spoken maybe forty sentences across four lessons, had said exactly one of them about parking, and she had been chewing on it since: "You back in from alongside the car in front, wheel toward the curb first, then away." She had nodded at the time without really seeing it, the way she nodded in calculus when a proof ended and everyone else looked satisfied.

She pulled alongside the sedan, checked her mirror, and reversed with the wheel turned toward the curb. The Honda crept in, nose still jutting toward the street, and stopped at an angle so obvious that a woman walking a terrier gave the car a wide, deliberate arc on the sidewalk. Savannah straightened, pulled out, and tried again without turning the wheel back. Same result: a diagonal, a wedge of car that belonged to no lane at all.

The third time, halfway into the space, she turned the wheel away from the curb, and the rear of the car swung so the nose came around, and suddenly she was level, close enough to the sedan that she could read the expired registration sticker. She sat with her hands on the wheel, breathing, then pulled forward and back until the tires kissed the curb. It had not felt like a trick. It had felt like two motions that needed each other, and she had only ever done the first one.

She was still sitting there when her phone buzzed. Her mother, from inside the bank: Are you coming in or not? Savannah locked the car and walked the half block, and it was only at the doors that she realized she had not thought about the parking once on the way, which was either progress or the beginning of forgetting.

Inside, the branch smelled like carpet cleaner and warm paper. Her mother was already at a teller's window with the deposit slip, and Savannah took the number for her own appointment, opening her first account with the eleven hundred dollars she had made lifeguarding. The clerk, a young guy with a lanyard, asked if she wanted overdraft protection, and her mother leaned over and said, "Tell her what that actually costs," and the guy, to his credit, did. Savannah listened to the fee schedule and thought about how the brochure in the lobby had made it sound like a kindness, a little umbrella held over you, and how the small print was where the umbrella got billed out from under you. She declined it. Her mother said nothing, which from her was applause.

On the walk back to the car, her mother asked how the parking had gone, and Savannah said, "I figured out the second turn." Her mother, who had failed her own test twice at eighteen and never let anyone in the family mention it, as though a failed test were something that could stigmatize a person for life, just nodded. Then, at the corner, she said, "Take the highway home."

"You said the merge scares you."

"It does. That's why."

The on-ramp rose in a long curve, and Savannah checked her mirror, then her blind spot, then the mirror again, the way Ruiz had shown her, looking for a gap she could walk the car into. A truck sat in the right lane like a verdict. Behind it, a space opened, and she pressed the accelerator and moved into it at the speed of traffic, and no one honked, and no one died, and the ordinary grace of that surprised her. Her mother's hand was flat on her knee, not gripping, just resting there, which was as close as she came to saying anything.

They rode in the flow of cars, and Savannah held her lane and thought, without wanting to, about how the parking and the merge were almost opposite instructions. In one you slowed down and gave ground and let the geometry work; in the other you committed, speed as a form of politeness. She could not yet say whether a good driver was someone who knew which situation demanded which, or someone who could feel the moment when one turned into the other. Probably the test next week would not ask her that. Probably the test would ask her to park between cones on a quiet street, and the cones would not care what she understood.

Her exit came up. She signaled early, checked the mirror, eased down the ramp with the wheel turned toward the curb of her own street waiting three lights ahead, and her mother said, "Same spot in front of the house. Show me again."

The community centre on Delmore Street smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and the room the mock court used had a water stain on the ceiling shaped, according to everyone who studied it, like either Ohio or a dog. Aidan had been assigned Tinker v. State of Ohio, a fictional case, but the packet Mrs. Okoye had photocopied included a page of real precedent, and at the top of that page, underlined twice by some previous student, was Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969.

He was supposed to argue both sides. That was the whole exercise. Eighteen minutes for the student who had been suspended after giving an angry speech on the courthouse steps, a speech that ended with the words "they should burn it down," and then, after a break for water and nerves, eighteen minutes against him. Aidan sat in a plastic chair with his notes on his lap and felt the peculiar foreboding of a person who suspects he will lose an argument with himself.

Priya, who had drawn the judging panel, leaned over the folding table that served as the bench. "Ready? Petitioner first. That's you, arguing the school can't punish the speech."

Aidan stood. His first draft had been all feeling, the kind of speech that had enraptured him when he wrote it at midnight, all righteousness and quotation marks, and he could see now why it would fail. So he started with the precedent instead. "Brandenburg v. Ohio, 1969," he said, and heard his voice steady the way it did when he stopped performing. "It held that advocating force can be punished only if it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action." He paused. "That's the test. It's called the imminent lawless action test."

"What's 'imminent' mean, exactly?" asked Marcus from the panel, chewing his pen.

"Like, now. Not someday. Not in theory." Aidan looked down at the facts he had invented and then been assigned to defend. "My client said 'they should burn it down.' He said it to forty people who were already leaving. Nobody had a match. The crowd was thinning out. Whatever he was advocating, it wasn't likely to produce anything that afternoon, because everybody was going home to dinner."

Priya scribbled something. It might have been "going home to dinner." It might have been a grocery list. That was the terror of the mock bench.

The break was three minutes. Aidan drank his water and then had to stand in front of the same chairs and take it all back, which felt, in a visceral and embarrassing way, like stepping on his own foot. "The state's position," he began, "is that this wasn't abstract advocacy. He named the building. He stood on its own steps. It was directed at inciting lawless action, and he had a crowd." He heard the words come out and recognized, with some horror, that he half believed them, or at least could believe them, the way you can believe a song in a language you don't speak.

"Half of them were walking away," Priya said, not unkindly.

"Walking away isn't the same as no likelihood," Aidan said. "That's my argument. It's not a great argument." He looked at the water stain, at Ohio or the dog. "Honestly, if you're asking me what I actually think, the Brandenburg test protects him, because 'should burn it down' is the kind of thing people say when they're angry, and the whole point of the test is that you can't punish angry words unless they're aimed at making something happen right then and likely to. But I'm supposed to be the state right now, so I'll keep going if you want."

Marcus lowered his pen. "Is that allowed? Arguing badly on purpose?"

"He's not arguing badly," Priya said. "He's arguing a side he doesn't hold. That's different." She shuffled her papers, and Aidan understood that she was granting him something, though he couldn't have named it. "Finish the rebuttal. You have four minutes."

He finished. He sat down with his heart going and his notes out of order, and Marcus leaned across the table and slid him the last of the coffee, which was cold and had a thumbprint in the lid. "You argued against yourself and won," Marcus said. "Or lost. Honestly, man, I can't tell which, and I was judging."

"That makes two of us," Aidan said, and drank the coffee anyway.

story:
Emile had promised his uncle he would run the tomato stall until noon, and he had promised the economics club he would come to Thursday's meeting with something to say about inflation. Both promises felt manageable at seven in the morning, when the market was cool and the baskets were full, and less so by nine, when Mrs. Okafor arrived and began, as she did every Saturday, to complain that his prices had gone up again.

"Two years ago these were a dollar fifty," she said, holding a Cherokee Purple up to the light like evidence in a trial.

"Fuel went up. The feed for the cover crop went up. My uncle says he's not making more, he's just keeping pace." Emile weighed the tomatoes without meeting her eye, because this was the exact argument he could not win, or even follow, and it was the reason he had nothing to say on Thursday.

"You're in that club at school, aren't you," Mrs. Okafor said. It wasn't a question. "The one where they argue about money. My grandson joined it, then quit. He said all they did was fight about the Federal Reserve."

At that moment Marcus came down the aisle carrying two coffees and a bag of peaches, wearing his club T-shirt with the supply curve printed on the back, which was how he dressed on Saturdays the way other people wore jerseys. He had been Emile's first friend at the school and the reason Emile had joined the club at all. He set one coffee on the crate beside the scale and said, "I heard that from three aisles away. Are you fighting about interest rates with a customer?"

"She started it," Emile said.

Mrs. Okafor paid for her tomatoes, exact change, and told Marcus that inflation was the government's fault and that someone ought to do something about it, and then she moved on to the honey stall, and the conversation was somehow his now.

Marcus leaned against the table and began his speech about Thursday's meeting, which Emile had missed for a dentist appointment. A sophomore named Priya had argued that if inflation rose one percentage point, the central bank only needed to raise its interest rate by one percentage point to answer it, a matching move, symmetrical and tidy. "And you know what Dev said to her?"

"I don't."

"He said that's exactly wrong. There's a thing called the Taylor rule, and it says when inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than that."

"More," Emile repeated. He thought of Mrs. Okafor's tomatoes, of his uncle recalculating prices every month, matching every increase and never getting ahead. "So it has to overshoot."

"That's the rule. I looked it up last night." Marcus bit into a peach with the satisfaction of someone who had stayed up past midnight for a principle.

Emile tried to hold both pictures at once: the club's clean diagram of a rate on a graph, and his uncle at the kitchen table sequestering receipts in a shoebox, doing the grim arithmetic of a small farm that borrowed money every spring. The rule made a strange kind of sense to him, the way it refused symmetry, and yet he could feel something in it that he couldn't yet name, some gap between the sentence Dev had quoted and the market stall they were standing at, where every rise in a price had a person behind it holding the fruit.

"Here's what I don't get," Emile said. "The rule says raise more than inflation. Fine. But somebody's loan gets more expensive when they do that. Some farmer's line of credit. Maybe my uncle's."

Marcus looked at him for a long moment, and Emile watched his friend arrive at the recognition that this was germane, that the meeting's argument and the stall's ledger were about the same thing, though neither of them had the language to connect them fully. "Priya would say that's not the point of the model."

"Priya's parents own the hardware store on Route 9," Emile said. "She knows exactly whose loans those are."

They were quiet while a woman with a stroller bought a basket of Romas and Emile made change, and the change itself felt like part of the argument, coins passing hand to hand, every transaction a small negotiation over what a dollar was worth this month versus last month. He understood now what he would say on Thursday: that he accepted the rule as stated, that raising by more than the rise was the only position he could defend, and that he still couldn't say what the right amount more was, or who paid for the overshoot. The uncertainty wasn't a hole in his argument. It was the argument.

"You'll come Thursday?" Marcus said, crumpling the peach bag.

"I'll come. I'll even wear the shirt."

"No you won't. You hate the shirt." Marcus grinned and pushed off the table, and Emile stacked the empty baskets, one inside another, and watched him go down the aisle toward the honey stall, where Mrs. Okafor was still holding forth.

story:
The whiteboard in the lodge said TIMELINE OF ALGORITHMS in Derek's block capitals, and beneath it a length of masking tape with index cards pinned along its length like birds on a wire. Abigail stood at the far end with a marker that was running dry, trying to figure out where her card belonged. The coding club had spent all of lunch arguing about which idea was oldest, Euclid's algorithm or the sieve or the fast Fourier transform, and Derek had decreed that everyone would place a card and defend it. Her card said BINARY SEARCH in her own handwriting, and beneath it she had written a question mark, because she did not actually know.

"Guess," Derek said from the picnic table, where he was trying to extrude the last of a glue stick onto a poster that had stopped mattering an hour ago. "That's the game."

"I don't guess in public," Abigail said. She pinned the card at 1950 with a shrug that fooled no one, and Priya, sitting cross-legged on the table with a laptop balanced on her knees, laughed without looking up.

"You're low," Priya said. "Way low."

"Then you place it."

"I already did. Quicksort, 1961. Tony Hoare. That one I know." Priya spun the laptop around. On the screen was a page about binary search, and Priya had the smug stillness of someone holding a card nobody else could see. "You want it or not?"

Abigail wanted it the way she wanted most things at that camp: quietly, and without anyone watching her reach. She took the laptop to the window, where the lake threw light up onto the ceiling, and read.

The number was smaller than she had guessed by a margin that embarrassed her. She read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to imply something strange. She had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that binary search was a modern trick, something that needed fast machines, the way you need a fast car before a road becomes worth building. The page said otherwise.

"Mauchly," she said aloud. "John Mauchly. 1946." She looked up. "It's from the Moore School Lectures."

"Which were what?" Derek asked, and she realized she had to answer carefully, because half the room was listening now and Priya was watching to see whether Abigail could hold what she had found.

"An early course on electronic computers. That's where the first known mention of binary search in computing shows up." She kept her voice flat, factual, and pinned the card in its new place, sliding Quicksort's card over to make room. 1946 sat there looking improbable, older than almost everything on the tape.

"First known," Priya said, tapping the phrase with one finger when she came over. "That's the loophole. Known. Something can be older than its first mention."

Abigail had already seen that, and had already started to distrust her own excitement. The fact was solid; what it meant was not. Maybe the idea had been obvious forever, halving the world to find one thing, the way you halve a phone book without being taught. Maybe Mauchly had only been the first to say it out loud to people who were building the machines that would need it. She could not decide, and she did not like not deciding, and she said so.

The obstreperous younger campers came through then, chasing a frisbee that clipped the edge of the timeline and sent two cards floating to the floor. Derek got loud. Abigail knelt and picked up her card and Priya's, and held them both, one in each hand, 1946 and 1961, and the small weight of fifteen years sat between her palms.

"Okay," Derek said, once the room had settled. "Placement defended. Now explain it to me like I'm stupid. Why does it beat just checking every item?"

That was the part Abigail had actually come to camp to learn, and she had been avoiding it all week. The instructor had shown them a sorted list and two functions and had moved on too fast, and Abigail had a private rule about moving on. She went to the dry-erase board, wrote out a list of the campers' cabin numbers, all twenty-four of them in order, and put her finger on the first one.

"Linear search. I check 1, then 2, then 3. Worst case I touch all of them." She moved her finger to the middle of the list. "Binary search. I jump here first. If the number I want is smaller, I forget the whole top half. If it's bigger, I forget the bottom half. Then I take the middle of what's left and do it again."

"So it's faster because you skip."

"No," Abigail said, and then stopped, because that was the wrong thing to say and she knew it the moment it left her. Derek's face closed. She tried again, slower. "It's faster because the skipping compounds. Every guess cuts what's left in half, so with twenty-four cabins I'm done in five guesses, not twenty-four. The gap gets huge as the list grows. A thousand cabins, and linear search is a thousand touches, and binary search is about ten."

Derek counted on his fingers, lips moving. Priya, who was something of a connoisseur of arguments and knew a genuine one when she heard it, leaned back against the window and watched Abigail the way people watch a high wire.

"Only on sorted data," Priya said. "That's the tax. You pay for the order first."

"Right," Abigail said. "It's not free. It's a trade." And that was the thing she had been turning over all afternoon, that the 1946 date and the halving trick were the same idea wearing different clothes: an old bargain between preparation and speed. You sort the world once so you can find things in it forever. She was not sure whether that made the idea old or new, whether Mauchly had invented it or merely noticed it, and she did not pretend to be sure, out loud or to herself.

"Fine," Derek said. He uncapped a fresh marker and wrote 1946 next to her card himself, pressing hard enough to squeak. "Defended. Next dispute, everybody, Euclid versus the sieve." He slapped the board twice. "Abigail, you're judge."

She picked up the marker he held out to her.

The basement smelled of damp carpet and microwave popcorn, and Deshad's laptop balanced on a milk crate between them. Loic had come over because the computer science placement exam was on Saturday, and because Deshad's mother made better snacks than anyone else's mother, though he would not have admitted the second reason in the vernacular of their friend group, where you showed up for the material and pretended the food was incidental.

"I don't get why it matters," Deshad said, scrolling through practice problems. "You look for the thing until you find the thing. That's a search. Done."

Loic pulled the laptop toward himself. "Say the list is sorted. A thousand names, alphabetical. You could start at the top and check every one." He typed a small demonstration, a loop crawling down an array, and watched the counter tick up: one, fourteen, ninety-two. "That's a linear search. But watch." He rewrote it, halved the range, halved it again. "Binary search. You jump straight to the middle, see which half your target is in, throw away the other half. Ten guesses, max, for a thousand items."

Deshad leaned back against the couch and ate a cold kernel of popcorn with the concentration of an epicurean sampling something rare. "Okay. That's actually satisfying. Like tearing a phone book in half."

Deshad's little sister Nia came halfway down the stairs, wrapped in a blanket, and stood there without saying anything. She had a essay due, Loic knew, and no laptop that worked, which was why Deshad had offered his old one. Deshad noticed her and pushed the popcorn bowl toward the bottom step without a word, and she took three pieces and stayed.

"Let's build it," Deshad said. "For real. I've got that contact list program from the summer. I'll add your binary search to it and it'll finally be fast."

He pulled up the project, and Loic read over his shoulder while the old machine warmed. The contacts lived in a linked list, one node pointing to the next, because that was the structure Deshad had learned first and trusted. Loic didn't say anything about it. He copied his binary search function into the file, wired it to the search box, and typed a name from the bottom of the alphabet.

The program hung. The little spinner turned, and turned, and Deshad reached over and jabbed the escape key. "It's slower than my old version," he said, sounding almost personally offended. "You said ten guesses."

Loic stared at the screen. He had promised elegance and delivered a crawl, and something about that destabilized him more than a wrong answer on homework ever had, because this was supposed to be his good idea, demonstrated in front of someone. He opened the profiler, then the data structure itself, following the pointers node by node. "It's still making ten guesses," he said slowly. "But every guess has to jump to the middle of what's left. In your list, you can't jump. To reach the middle you have to walk through the items one by one, from the front."

"So the walk eats the savings."

"The walk eats the savings." Loic sat back. "The whole trick is jumping straight to the middle. On an array you can jump anywhere. On a linked list, the middle is as far away as the end is." He was quiet for a second, then laughed, short and embarrassed. "I was so proud of the halving I forgot to ask what it was standing on."

Nia spoke from the stairs, around her popcorn. "So is it a bad algorithm?"

"No," Loic said. "It's a good algorithm in the wrong neighborhood." He glanced at Deshad. "We could rebuild the contacts as an array. Or keep the linked list and use the old slow search, because with two hundred names it honestly doesn't matter."

Deshad considered this, chin on his fist. He changed his mind the way he usually did, all at once. "Rebuild it. If we're doing this, I want the fast one, done right, not the fast one bolted onto the wrong thing." He pulled his chair closer to Loic's and started deleting the node declarations.

They worked until almost ten, Deshad typing, Loic reading each change aloud, Nia drifting the rest of the way down the stairs to sit on the bottom step with the blanket pooled around her, occasionally pointing at a typo. Twice they broke the program entirely and had to retrace. When they finally ran the search, the result appeared before the spinner could finish its first rotation, and Deshad made a small sound of delight and saved the file three separate times, which was his habit whenever something mattered.

Deshad's mother called down that it was late. Nia gathered her blanket and, on her way up, paused long enough to say, "Good luck Saturday," and Loic said thanks, though he was no longer sure luck was the operative word. He closed the laptop lid but did not yet put on his shoes. He was thinking about all the other clever things he had memorized without asking where they applied, and how many wrong neighborhoods he might be standing in without knowing.

"One more game of pool before you go?" Deshad said, racking the balls.

story:
The 6:40 bus carried the smell of wet jackets and diesel, and Elijah sat near the back with a stack of index cards on his knee. On each card, in his narrow handwriting, was a question he had copied from a library book called Getting Hired at Sixteen: Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team. Tell me about a time you handled a deadline. Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult person. The interview at Hendrick's Market was Saturday morning, and this was the last ride he'd have to practice, so he held the cards low, out of the driver's mirror, and answered under his breath.

Before he'd left the house he'd called Dana, who had the same book out of the same library and had read ahead. "They're behavioral questions," she'd said. "The whole chapter's about them." Then she'd read him the line from the page, slowly, like it was scripture: behavioral interview questions, such as "Tell me about a time when," are built on the idea that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior. Elijah had written it on the back of his first card, mostly because it sounded important, partly because it sounded like a problem. He had no past behavior. He had never bagged a groat, never run a register, never been late to a shift because there had never been a shift.

He tried the team question first. "Tell me about a time you worked as part of a team," he murmured, and the boreal wind leaking through the window seal made the cards flutter. The only team he could think of was the ninth-grade geography project, the one where Marcus had promised to build the glacier model and then hadn't, so Elijah had stayed up two nights molding mashed newspaper into ice while his mother asked, from the doorway, whether this was really a one-person assignment. He said it out loud, quietly, angled so the woman beside him couldn't hear: "I covered for a teammate and I got the project in on time." It came out flat, like a lie, even though it was true.

Between his stop and the school he turned the sentence over. He could tell the story two ways. In one, he was the reliable one, the rescuer, and that made him sound like someone a manager would want. In the other, he was the boy who had covered for Marcus and then said nothing to the teacher, which was loyalty or cowardice depending on how you looked at it, and he couldn't adjudicate between those two verdicts even for himself. He had never decided, in two years, whether he'd done right. He only knew that Marcus had said "you're a lifesaver" and then sat with different people at lunch by December, and that the glacier had gotten an A minus, the minus for lopsidedness.

Across the aisle, in the seat by the rear door, a man in a green canvas coat had been dozing with his chin on his chest, and he was not dozing anymore. His name was Augustine Okafor, and he was the one who conducted the interviews at Hendrick's Market, the one whose signature would sit at the bottom of Elijah's hire or non-hire. He had heard the boy rehearsing, "tell me about a time," over and over, voice pitched low, and he had heard the glacier story twice, getting slightly different each time. In the first version the teammate had merely forgotten. In the second the teammate had been at his cousin's party the whole weekend. Augustine found he preferred the second.

He had sat through four hiring seasons of sixteen-year-olds and could predict, from the first answer, how the whole interview would go. The rehearsed ones delivered their answers like the school announcements, eyes on a middle distance where no one lived. What he could not predict, what no reference checked, was what a kid did on the days no one was scoring him. He thought of his own first interview, decades ago, at a warehouse in a colder city, and how he had made up an answer about teamwork because he assumed that was the price of entry, and how the manager had known, he was sure now, and hired him anyway. That had never stopped being strange to him.

Saturday came gray and cold, and Elijah walked to Hendrick's in his father's tie, knotted twice because the tie was made for a wider man. The back office smelled of cardboard and oranges. Augustine Okafor sat behind a desk with a folder open, and the green canvas coat was hanging on the door, and Elijah did not recognize it, because he had never once looked at the face of the sleeping man near the rear door.

"Tell me about a time," Augustine said, "when you had to depend on someone, and it went wrong."

Elijah's cards were in his backpack, but the question was close enough to his practiced ones that the glacier rose in him immediately, whole, in its proper chronology: the assignment, the promise, the party, the two nights of newspaper, the A minus. He could feel both versions in his mouth, the tidy one and the true one, and the true one included the part he'd never settled, that he hadn't told the teacher and still wasn't sure he should have. "There was a project," he said, and then he looked up, at Augustine's actual eyes, which was a thing he had practiced in the bathroom mirror and never once managed. "My partner didn't do his part. I did it for him. I didn't say anything to anyone, and I've gone back and forth about that ever since, honestly."

There was a pause long enough for the radiator to click twice. Augustine leaned back. "You take the 6:40," he said. "Northbound. You sit near the back door."

Elijah felt his face go hot, the whole ride rearranging itself in his mind, every muttered rehearsal suddenly public, the second version of the glacier overheard by the one person whose verdict mattered. "You were," he started, and couldn't finish it.

"I was," Augustine said. He turned the folder ninety degrees on the desk, though it was empty, and clicked his pen once. "Tell me the part about the teacher again. Slower this time."

The canoe had to be fixed by Friday, and Prue's steering was the problem, though Juliette had not yet found a way to say so. They were training for the camp's end-of-summer race, two paddlers per boat, and their times had stalled at third-best out of six crews. Juliette, who liked numbers more than she liked most people, had graphed their splits on graph paper torn from the back of her binder. The numbers were not ambiguous. On the portage and the flats they were fast. In the last turn before the finish, Prue crossed her stroke early and they lost two seconds to the wall of reeds.

She had tried kindness already, in the form of a speech on Tuesday. She had said the turn was great, the rhythm was great, the pull through the shallows was honestly beautiful, and then, at the very end, like a pebble dropped into a lake, "maybe just hold the rudder a half-beat longer." Prue had gone quiet the whole paddle back to the dock. At dinner she sat with the girls from Cabin 4 and did not look over. The five good things had evaporated; the one small bad thing had swollen to fill the tent.

That night Juliette lay awake in the foamy dark and thought about a review she had found in June, in a psychology textbook her sister left behind before her furlough from the pediatric ward, three weeks of forced rest that she spent mostly repotating the porch. The chapter cited a 2001 review led by Roy Baumeister, called "Bad Is Stronger Than Good," and its finding was simple and slightly depressing: negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size. Even, the review implied, when the positive ones outnumbered them five to one. Which was exactly the ratio Juliette had deployed on the dock, with exactly the wrong result. She had assumed praise worked like ballast, weighing down the criticism so it couldn't capsize anything. Apparently it worked more like water off a duck.

"I read something," she said to Prue the next morning, the lake still flat and pewter-colored, their canoe overturned on the racks for the waxing they did before each session. "A 2001 review. Roy Baumeister led it. It's called 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good.'"

"Is this you telling me I'm bad?"

"It's me telling you I did the math wrong on Tuesday. Not the turn math. The people math." Juliette turned the canoe over; a spider fled along the gunwale. "If bad hits harder than good, then burying the bad at the end of five nice things doesn't soften it. It just means you hear it last, alone, with all the nice stuff already forgotten."

Prue took the wax cloth and started on the stern without answering. Her shoulders had a way of organizing themselves into a verdict. Finally she said, "So what's the plan, you just open with the bad part?"

"Open with it, make it small, make it about one thing, and then let the rest of the day be normal. And I say the good things separately, later, when they're their own events. Not packing material."

"Parametrize me, then," Prue said, wringing out the cloth. It was a word she'd stolen from Juliette over the campfire and used wrong half the time, but this time she pointed at the graph paper tucked under the seat. "You've got the whole week on that page. Where do I break?"

Juliette unfolded the paper against the hull. "The last turn, every run. You cross your stroke maybe half a second early. That's it. That's the entire bad thing. Everything else is the fastest I've ever paddled with anybody."

The rest they worked out on the water. Prue counted her stroke aloud through the turn, "and, and, and, hold," and the first time she did it they clipped the reeds anyway, and she laughed, an actual laugh, which Juliette had not heard since Tuesday. The second time they missed them by a boat's width. The third time the turn was clean and Prue whooped so loudly that a heron lifted off from the far bank with an air of deep personal grievance.

On Thursday, at the dessert line during the camp's half-hedonistic banquet night, when even the counselors were having seconds of the fudge, Juliette said, "Your pull through the shallows is the strongest in the fleet. I've been meaning to tell you that on its own, not stapled to anything."

Prue considered this over her second square of fudge. "It's weird," she said, "I actually believe you this time."

Race day came gray and then bright. They took the turn clean, crossed second, and lost overall to Cabin 3 by four seconds, which was closer than the graph paper had predicted. Juliette couldn't decide whether the method had worked or whether Prue had simply improved out of spite, and she said so on the paddle back. Prue shipped her paddle and let the boat drift.

"Spite, math, whatever," she said. "Same water." Then she dipped her hand in over the side and flicked it at Juliette, once, deliberately, and waited to see what Juliette would say about that.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
Antoine arrived at the book club twelve minutes early, which was a form of subterfuge, because what he wanted was ten uninterrupted minutes with the photocopied chapter before anyone could ask him what he thought of it. The club met in the back room of a shuttered travel agency that Priya's aunt leased for storage, six folding chairs and a card table under a fluorescent panel that buzzed like something trapped. He had read the chapter three times at home and understood, in the way you understand a weather report, that it was about a misunderstanding between two people of consequence, and now he needed it to be about something he could actually say out loud.

Priya arrived with a thermos and her copy folded into quarters. "You started without us," she said, though there was nothing yet to start without.

"I was counting," Antoine said.

"Counting what?"

He turned the photocopy toward her, where the margins were already dark with his pencil. "The servants. In this chapter alone they're named eleven times. Bessie, and the cook, and the man who drives the carriage. Eleven times they're mentioned." He paused, unsure whether the next part would sound clever or insane. "They speak twice. Two lines, total. One of them is 'Yes, miss.'"

Priya sat down slowly, the way people do when they're deciding whether to be interested. "So?"

"So the whole book is like that. There's always someone carrying something up a staircase, or lighting a fire before anyone wakes up, and the story just walks past them." He had been half asleep in history class when Ms. Okonkwo had said that a Marxist reading often asks whose labour makes the characters' comfortable lives possible, and he had written it on his wrist because he had no paper, and the words had survived two showers and looked, by now, like a scar. He didn't mention the wrist. He said, "Whose labour makes their comfort possible. That's the question. And the answer is standing in the doorway the whole novel, holding a tray."

The others arrived in a scatter: Marcus with his skateboard, Delia with the flu, Sahil with the information that he hadn't finished the chapter, which he offered as though it were a contribution. When Priya relayed Antoine's count, Sahil frowned at his own copy and started tallying on his own, tongue between his teeth, and came up with eleven and two as well, which felt to Antoine like the first time all year that a number he'd produced had survived contact with another person.

"That's not a flaw in the book, though," Delia said, blowing her nose. "It's how the world was. Brontë's writing what she sees."

"But she sees it," Antoine said, and heard his own voice climb, and lowered it. "That's what gets me. She notices them enough to name them, eleven times, and not once enough to let them matter. It's not that the servants aren't there. It's that they're furniture that can talk, and the book decides twice per chapter to let them."

Marcus turned his skateboard over on his knees. "Okay, but the novel's about Jane. If every servant got a subplot you'd have a different book."

"That's exactly the question," Antoine said. "Is it? Or is the book's whole idea of who deserves a story built on the ones it never has to pay attention to?" He had assumed, walking over, that the argument would be about whether the lens was fair to a dead novelist. What he found instead, sitting there, was that he liked the novel more with the lens on, not less, that the silences he'd skated over were now load-bearing, that they underpinned every scene he'd loved, and he couldn't tell whether that was insight or a kind of betrayal. He said none of this. He said, "I'm not saying we throw it out. I'm saying we read the gaps on purpose."

"For someone who came in counting," Priya said, "you're very sure it's not just arithmetic."

He laughed, and it came out rougher than he meant. "I'm not sure. That's the honest version. I can see what the lens shows and I can see what it hides. It hides, like, everything Jane feels. The whole interior of the book. So either the feelings are the point and the servants are the price, or the servants are the point and the feelings are the subterfuge, and I don't know which, and I think admitting that is allowed."

It was nearly nine when they packed up. Delia's mother was honking outside, and Sahil stacked the chairs with the efficiency of a boy who wanted to be gone. Priya's aunt appeared in the doorway with a ring of keys, waiting without complaint while they gathered cups, and Antoine realized he had been in this room two hours and had not once wondered who swept it, who paid for its light, whether she was paid for waiting.

He picked up the last two cups and carried them to her. "I can lock up if you want," he said.

She looked at him, keys in hand, deciding.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
story:
The basement smelled like solder and the ghost of someone's older brother's cigarettes, and Andrew had claimed the good folding chair by rights of having carried the mini-fridge down the stairs himself. Priya sat cross-legged on the carpet with her laptop balanced on a biology textbook she'd never opened, and Marcus was doing that thing he did when code broke, which was staring at the screen as if it owed him money.

"The lookup is slow again," Marcus said. "Watch." He dragged his finger across the trackpad, and the parts finder took a beat, then another, before returning the row for a single 8mm standoff. "That's three seconds. For one standoff."

"Tragic," Priya said. "Hold a funeral."

Andrew leaned over anyway, because the parts finder was his fault in the first place, or half his fault. Their robotics team had inherited two functions from last year's seniors: one that walked the sorted parts list from the top until it found what it wanted, and one nobody used because it was commented in another language, literally, the comments were in Polish. Andrew had spent two evenings translating them. The function was called a binary search, and the seniors had left it sitting there like a gift nobody unwrapped.

"Put it in," Andrew said. "Swap it in and time it."

Marcus already had the timing harness up, because Marcus loved measuring things more than he loved building them. He ran both functions against the current parts list, four hundred entries, and the two times came back nearly identical. He looked at Andrew with an expression of profound, theatrical disappointment. "Congratulations. You translated Polish for nothing."

"It's not nothing, it's, hang on." Andrew pulled the laptop closer. The whole reason the finder had gotten slow was that Coach Okafor had dumped a second supplier's catalog into their spreadsheet overnight, and the list had gone from four hundred entries to about eight hundred, because of course it had, two weeks before the regional. Andrew ran both functions again. The old one, the one that walked the list from the top, had roughly doubled the time it took in the worst case, which Marcus announced in the tone of a weather reporter delivering news of a hurricane. The translated one, the binary search, had gotten slower by what looked like one step. One. Andrew ran it three more times to be sure it wasn't the laptop breathing hard.

"That's a rounding error," Marcus said.

"It's not a rounding error, it's the whole point." Andrew was talking faster now, the way he did when something snapped together in his head and he had to say it before it dissolved. "Watch what happens when the list doubles. The old one doubles its worst-case work. Every time. The new one adds one step. That's why the seniors wrote it. That's why the comments are in Polish and still, somehow, smarter than us."

Priya put her hand up like they were in a classroom. "Explain it like I'm a person who has a biology textbook and no idea what you just said."

So Andrew did the thing he'd been practicing without knowing he was practicing it, which was explaining. He had the sorted list open, and he kept his hands still, because his dad always said talking with your hands made people seasick. "The old function starts at the top and checks every row until it finds the part. Sorted doesn't help it at all. The new one uses the fact that the list is sorted. Doubling the list only costs it one extra step." He pointed at the numbers on the screen. "Eight hundred entries, and the worst case is, it's barely more than it was at four hundred. Meanwhile the old one's worst case doubled overnight, exactly when Coach doubled the list."

"That is genuinely mesmerizing," Priya said, and she meant it, which Andrew could tell because she stopped scrolling her phone. "It's like the list is a boreal forest and you're not hiking through it, you're flying over it."

"That metaphor does not survive contact with computer science," Marcus said, "but I accept it anyway."

What Andrew did not say, because he was still working out how to say it, was the part that had been bothering him since the translation. He'd spent the whole summer between high school and this gap year reading arguments about whether understanding a thing and being able to use a thing were the same, and the pragmatics of it felt slippery in his hands. He could explain the doubling rule with the screen in front of him. He could not yet explain, in a way that satisfied him, why the rule felt different from the other stuff he'd memorized for tests and immediately lost. Maybe it was that he'd watched it happen instead of being told. Maybe it was that the seniors had left the thing untranslated, a small locked door, and he'd had to want it. He didn't know. He said some of this out loud, carefully, the way you test a bridge with one foot.

"So you don't know why you understand it," Priya said.

"I know that I understand it. I don't fully know what understanding is. Those are different problems and I'm only solving one of them tonight."

"That's the most Andrew sentence ever spoken in this basement," Marcus said, "and this basement has heard you defend the metric system for forty minutes."

They swapped the binary search into the parts finder properly, all call sites, and committed it. Then, because it was eleven at night and nobody had homework that couldn't be ignored until Sunday, Marcus generated a fake parts list with a hundred thousand entries and ran both functions on it. The old one sat there grinding while he narrated its suffering in a nature-documentary whisper. The new one came back before he finished his sentence about the endurance of the humble linear search.

Andrew copied the timing numbers into the team's shared doc, then sat back and looked at the two columns, one growing like a weed, one barely moving. "Next year's team is going to find our comments in English," he said. "Boring, but fair." Priya reached over and added, at the top of the function, one line of Polish she'd typed from a translation app: "Dokładnie tak." Exactly so.
