activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
story:
I never told anyone at school that I spent my Sunday mornings in the basement of Beth Shalom arguing about roofs. It sounded either grandiose or embarrassing, depending on who you asked, and I preferred neither. That morning Rabbi Taragin had given us photocopied pages of Deuteronomy and told us to find one law we thought was dead and one we thought was alive, and to defend both from the text itself, no googling, no quoting rabbis we hadn't read.

I already knew which verse I wanted, which is probably why I missed what actually happened in the room.

I found it fast, Deuteronomy 22:8, the command to build a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house. What I remembered from Hebrew school was that the tradition doesn't leave it stuck on rooftops; it stretches outward to other hazards on one's property. What I wanted to argue was that the synagogue's back stairwell, the one down to the social hall with the loose second-floor banister, was exactly the kind of thing the verse had in mind. Not literally a roof. But the same idea, the same obligation.

I stood up too fast and my chair scraped. "The verse isn't about roofs," I said. "It's about the fact that your building can hurt somebody, and if you know it can, you have to act. The rabbis took the parapet rule and extended it to other hazards on your property. A broken banister counts. We should fix it before the high holidays, when the building fills up with people who don't know where the loose rail is."

Rabbi Taragin folded his hands, which I took, at the time, as dismissal.

Before that Sunday there had been a Tuesday I kept replaying. My grandmother had come down her porch steps holding a casserole and caught her heel where the bottom tread had rotted through, and I had watched the dish go one way and her body go the other, and the whole ride to the emergency room I kept thinking that somebody must have known, that wood doesn't rot overnight. When she got her cast, she waved off the stairs like they were nothing, and that made it worse. I had decided, in the hospital waiting room, that knowing about a hazard and doing nothing was the actual sin. Then I had looked for proof, and found a verse three thousand years old, sitting there the whole time.

So when Rabbi Taragin folded his hands, I heard the sermon he never gave. I heard him say the law was of its time, that flat roofs were flat roofs, that a teenager with a photocopied page should probably sit down. I sat down. I did not hear what he actually said, because I had stopped listening, which is a thing I only understood later.

Later came in the car, because Danny Felsen, who had transcribed the whole discussion into his notebook like it was a courtroom record, read his notes back to me when I asked him to. He did it without ceremony, the way he does everything, his finger moving under his own cramped handwriting. According to Danny, Rabbi Taragin had said, "That's a strong reading. Who can find where the tradition first extends it beyond the roof?" According to Danny, I had said, "It's obvious," and put my head down on the table for the last twenty minutes. According to Danny, the rabbi had asked me twice, by name, to continue, and I had said I was tired.

Here is what Danny could not know, writing his faithful little record. When I was eleven my mother ran for the school board, and I stood in the gym during the vote count believing that whoever spoke most confidently would win the plebiscite, and my mother, who spoke quietly, lost, and afterward told me the counting had been the easy part. I had decided then that folding hands and speaking softly meant someone was being polite about burying you. It was a bad generalization and I had kept it for seven years, and it had sat there in that basement classroom deciding what I heard.

The next Sunday I came back with a photograph of my grandmother's porch steps on my phone and a copy of the verse, and I asked Rabbi Taragin if I could start over. He said the tradition calls the broader obligation a fence, a fence around the law, and I said no, that wasn't the part I meant, I meant the parapet itself, and he smiled and said, then build your case.

What I said, standing at the table this time instead of standing over it, was that I couldn't prove the banister was my responsibility, only that it was somebody's, and that the verse seemed less interested in who than in whether. I said the honest limit of my argument was that I was motivated by a porch in Ramsey, not by Deuteronomy, and maybe that was backwards, and maybe it wasn't, and I didn't know yet how to tell. Danny wrote it all down anyway.

The building committee met on a Thursday. They voted to fix the rail, but not before the holidays, because bids take time, and because one member, Mr. Alper, wanted to check whether the repair required a permit. My grandmother's steps are still rotted; she told me not to nag her, and I haven't found the argument that changes that, in any text, yet.

On my way out I passed the stairwell and put my hand on the loose rail, and it moved under my palm, just slightly, like something deciding.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
Kaylee arrived at Mrs. Ferreira's studio ten minutes early, which meant she sat in the hallway outside the door listening to the previous student play the same Mozart movement she had been assigned, a C major sonata movement from a book that smelled like her grandmother's attic. She had the score open on her knees, three colored pencils clipped to the cover like a bookmark, and a page of Mrs. Ferreira's instructions folded into her back pocket: mark the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation, and be ready to say why she put the lines where she did.

"You're going to argue with me," Mrs. Ferreira said when it was Kaylee's turn. She was heating water for tea on a hot plate that had a burn ring shaped like Australia on it. "Everyone argues at this stage. It's a rite."

"I don't argue," Kaylee said. "I negotiate."

Mrs. Ferreira had her own agenda, which she mentioned while rinsing the teapot. Her recital was in three weeks, and she wanted to program the second half of the same concert with student performances, which meant she wanted Kaylee ready for an audience, not just for a grade. "So think of today as both things," she said. "Analysis and rehearsal. They feed each other, in theory."

Kaylee set the score on the rack and played the opening, then stopped where she had drawn the first pencil line. "Exposition starts here, obviously. First theme, C major." She played on until a new tune arrived, lighter, hopping, clearly a different character. This was where she had stopped the night before and stared at the page for twenty minutes. In her headphones it felt like the music had changed rooms without telling her. So she had checked the key signature on the score, and there it was, one sharp where there had been none. "The second theme is in G," she said. "The whole exposition moves to the dominant. C major goes to G major, that's just what happens, that's where the new tune lives."

"And your other pencil marks?"

"The development starts here," Kaylee said, playing the measure, "because the material starts breaking apart, it stops being themes and starts being pieces of them." She had drawn that line confidently. The third line, the one that closed the recapitulation, she had drawn, erased, and redrawn four times. She played the passage and let it hang in the room. "I put it here. But I'm not sure. It comes back in C, the first theme comes back, so recapitulation, but there's this little bit before it that might belong to either side. I keep moving it."

Mrs. Ferreira drank her tea and did not rescue her. "Play it three ways," she said. "Line before the little bit, line after it, no line at all, you just pretend the question doesn't exist."

"That third one's tempting," Kaylee said, and played it. In the studio's dry acoustic the passage sounded smaller than it did in her headphones, less dramatic, almost a shrug. She played it again with the line placed after, and the little bit suddenly sounded like a hinge, a thing that existed to be opened. She sat back. "Okay. It's after. But I want to say the part I can't prove. I think it works both ways, and the reason I'm choosing after is the key. When the music gets back to C, and stays there, that's home. The little bit is still deciding."

"You realize you just made an argument and then told me it might be wrong," Mrs. Ferreira said.

"I made an argument and told you which part of it is load-bearing and which part is hope," Kaylee said. "That's different."

Mrs. Ferreira laughed into her teacup. "Fine. For the recital, you'll say the second part only. An audience wants the argument, not your doubts. They metabolize the doubt anyway, whether you serve it or not." She tapped the score. "But keep the full version somewhere. In here," and she touched the margin of the page with one finger, "the way geologists keep the sedimentary layers. Everything you thought along the way, stacked in order."

"That's a lot of pencil in one margin," Kaylee said.

"That's why I gave you three colors."

Kaylee played the movement through from the top, stopping only at the second theme to glance down at the single sharp and confirm, again, the change of room. When she finished, Mrs. Ferreira was standing at the shelf pulling recital programs from a box, already counting chairs.

"Half the second half," she said. "That's you. Wear something without a logo."

"Logos," Kaylee said. "As in a word."

"As in a corporate identity plastered across your chest. Same root, different customer." Mrs. Ferreira handed her a program blank and a pen. "Write your own bio. Two sentences. Make the first one true."

Kaylee sat down on the piano bench with the blank page and wrote her name at the top, then stopped, pen hovering, and read the margin of her score instead, all three colors of it, before she began.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
story:
The laptop belonged to Mathis's brother, and it had to be back in his brother's dorm room by six o'clock, which meant Mathis had four hours to finish something he had promised the robotics club he could finish. He spread his things across the corner table on the second floor of the public library, beside the tall window where the afternoon light fell on a squat gray paperweight that the librarian claimed was a chunk of igneous rock hauled down from some mountain quarry. The club had been polite about his application. Polite, and then clear: build a working class in Java, private fields, getter methods, and tests that pass, and bring it Thursday. They did not say what would happen if he brought nothing, which was somehow worse than saying it.

He started with the fields. A Book class, because it was a library and because he could not think of anything less embarrassing to be caught writing. Private String title. Private String author. Private double price. He had learned the pattern from a forum post of uncertain provenance, a snippet someone had pasted without saying where they found it, and Mathis had spent a whole evening deciding whether to trust it. His brother's advice, offered over the phone with a mouthful of dinner, was different: trust the compiler, not the internet. His friend Dee's advice was the opposite. Read everything, she said, before you touch the keyboard. He was trying to suture the two approaches together, taking structure from the forum and caution from Dee, checking each line before moving to the next.

The constructor came easily. Getters came easily too, small doors opening onto the private rooms he had built. Then he hit the tests, and the tests were where the afternoon began to go wrong.

He wrote a JUnit test the way the forum snippet showed, called the getter, and compared it against the number he expected. He ran it. Red. Failure. That was the moment the clock on the wall above the reference desk started to matter, because the failure message did not say what he thought it would say.

He read it three times. Expected: 24.99. Actual: 14.99. He sat back and pressed his palms against his eyes. Fourteen ninety-nine was the price he had passed to the constructor, the price he had typed himself, and he was certain of it the way you are certain of your own birthday. Twenty-four ninety-nine was the number he had wanted, the number in his head, the one he had placed in the test believing it belonged there. The machine seemed to have them exactly backwards, insisting it had expected the number he knew he'd supplied, and reporting as "actual" the number he knew he'd only hoped for. He checked the constructor. He checked the field. He checked the getter, character by character, and the ticking of the wall clock got louder, or at least that was how it felt, and the light on the gray igneous paperweight shifted a few degrees as the sun moved.

A girl two tables over was also coding, headphones around her neck, and she had been muttering at her screen for the last ten minutes. Now she said, to no one in particular but loudly enough to be an invitation, "Why does it keep saying it expected the wrong number? That's the number I gave it."

"Show me," Mathis said, before he had decided to say anything.

She brought her laptop over. Her test was red too, a failed assertEquals on some total she was computing, and her failure message had the same inverted quality as his, insisting on an expectation that didn't match what she believed she'd expected. They sat with the two red messages side by side, hers and his, and Mathis read them again, slowly, the way Dee had told him to read everything before touching anything.

"Wait," he said. He highlighted one of the lines. "What if the first thing you put in there isn't yours? What if it's the one you wanted all along, and the second one is what your code actually made? Expected first, actual second."

She stared at the line. "So when I swapped them, I swapped the meaning too."

"And the message," Mathis said. "The message follows the order."

She corrected her arguments. Green. She laughed once, short and surprised, and went back to her table.

Mathis did not fix his own test right away. He sat looking at his red message, at the number he had supplied and the number he had only wanted, and he thought about his brother's advice and Dee's advice, which had seemed like opposites all week and now seemed like two hands on the same tool. Trust the compiler, but read what it actually says, not what you assume it means. He could not have proven which advice had saved him, or whether both had, and he let that stay uncertain, because Thursday was coming and six o'clock was coming faster.

He reversed the two arguments in his assertEquals, ran the test, and watched the bar turn green. Then he ran the whole suite, four tests, all green, and started copying the files to his flash drive with the window light gone amber behind him.

A message appeared from his brother: It's 5:45. Where's my laptop?

Mathis closed the lid, zipped the case, and texted back with his thumb while walking. "On my way. Everything passed."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Hannah arrived at the market before seven, when the vendors were still unstacking crates and the grass in the square held the night's damp. In her backpack, wrapped in two dish towels, she carried a pound of dark couverture and a rubber spatula, and beneath the weight of those ordinary things, something harder to name. She was here to prove a choice: that she could keep her mother's stall, the one she had inherited rather than earned, or at least that she could stand in it one Saturday without pretending.

Ruth, who sold cheese two tables down and had known Hannah's mother for fifteen years, nodded at her over a wheel of something sharp. "You're early," Ruth said, which was all, but the tone carried the rest. You're here, then. You didn't sell the equipment after all. Hannah lifted a hand in answer and kept walking.

The stall smelled of old cocoa butter, ghost of a hundred batches. Hannah set up the marble slab first, because that was the thing her mother had guarded like a relic, a broad cool stone she'd bought before Hannah was born. Her mother had never taught her the tempering. That was the wound Hannah had decided not to examine, most days, and today was not most days. She unwrapped the chocolate and began chopping it into even pieces, the knife knocking a rhythm against the board while the sky behind the church tower went from grey to a pale, unhopeful blue.

She melted the chocolate in a bowl set over the small burner, stirring, watching the glossy pool thin and loosen. Her friend Dev had tried this at his house last month, on the cold stone counter in his mother's kitchen, and had texted her afterward in fragments: spread it out, work it around, let the stone pull the heat out of it. He called it tabling. "It's called tabling," he'd said on the phone, laughing at the plainness of the word, "you literally put it on the table, more or less, a marble one, and you move it around until it thickens up right." Dev's attempt had failed, his chocolate blooming white and streaked by morning, but he had described the marble under his palms so exactly, the shock of the cold, that Hannah had felt she was already half-taught.

She poured a pool of the melted chocolate onto the slab. The stone received it with an audible hiss of heat leaving, and Hannah began to work it with the spatula, spreading it wide, scraping it back, spreading it again. The chocolate moved like something deciding. At the edges it lost its shine and dulled, and she gathered that dull chocolate back into the center and kept folding, and the whole mass began, slowly, to thicken and cling. She understood, with her hands before her head, that she was cooling it, yes, but also starting something inside it, coaxing the right kind of structure into being, though what that structure was she could not have said and did not try to.

"You're doing it," Ruth said, arriving beside her with two coffees. She held one out. Above them the awning's shadow lay across the slab, and the early sun behind the church began to adumbrate the shapes of the market's opening hour, long diagonal shadows of crates and umbrellas crossing the cobbles toward the stalls. "Your mother used to do that exactly like that. The little turn at the end."

Hannah kept her eyes on the chocolate. "She never showed me," she said. "She said I'd learn it when I needed to."

"And do you need to?"

"I don't know yet. I sold the molds last week. I kept the marble." She said it flatly, letting the contradiction sit there between them like the slab itself, something neither of them was going to polish smooth. Ruth sipped her coffee and did not rescue her from it, which Hannah recognized, distantly, as a kindness.

The chocolate on the marble reached the moment Dev had described and she had not believed: it held a clean edge when the spatula lifted, and when she drew the tip through it, the line stayed. She scraped it back into the warm bowl, combined it, and dipped the corner of a sheet of parchment, watching the coated strip set. It hardened within a minute, and she broke it. The snap was short and definite, a sound like a small lock closing, and the surface shone.

The first customers were drifting in now, a man weighing tomatoes, a woman arguing cheerfully with the honey seller about whether the wildflower could really be called autochthonous to the valley or whether the bees had simply made do, as bees do. Ruth drifted back to her cheeses. Hannah stood behind her mother's table with a tray of tempered chocolate beginning to form, and she thought about Dev's text from that failed night, sent at two in the morning: if it never sets, if it's always just going to be a soft blob, then what's the point, this is basically nihilism. She had laughed at it then. Standing here now, she thought the opposite might be truer, that the whole craft was a small argument against that softness, though she could not have said whether her mother would agree, or whether her mother had kept the tempering from her on purpose or out of sheer habit of doing everything herself. That stayed unresolved, and she let it.

A girl of maybe ten stopped at the table, coins counted out in advance in her fist, staring at the tray where the chocolate was setting in even, shining squares. "Is it real?" the girl asked.

"It snaps," Hannah said, and broke a piece to show her.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
The restaurant was called Le Petit Moulin, and Zoe's aunt let her sit at the corner table on Tuesday nights because Tuesdays were slow and the table by the window was otherwise empty. Zoe spread out her French homework there: a printed article from Le Monde about rising rents in Paris, a dictionary, and a notebook with a vocabulary list that had grown to four pages. Her tutor, Marceline, worked the Tuesday shift, and between tables she would come over, tap the page, and listen.

"Read me the first paragraph," Marceline said, setting down a glass of water she hadn't been asked for. "Out loud. Then tell me in French what it says."

Zoe began. The first sentence went all right, but by the third she was drowning. The article was about "la pression immobilière," and Zoe did not know whether that meant pressure on buildings or pressure from them, and the sentence about young workers leaving the city had a clause inside a clause that she could not find her way out of. She stopped, looked up, and admitted she had lost the thread.

"C'est trop dur," Marceline said, not unkindly. "Too hard. For you, right now."

Zoe argued, a little, because she had chosen the article on purpose. Her French teacher had offered the class a choice: an easy text from the textbook, or a real article from a real newspaper, worth more credit. Zoe had taken the harder path the way she took most hard paths, with a private exhilaration that arrived before the actual work did and never lasted through it. Now every paragraph felt like a puzzle whose pieces belonged to three different boxes. She had assumed that if she looked up enough words, the meaning would assemble itself. It had not. It was like stirring a river; the water stayed turbid no matter how long she went at it with a spoon.

Marceline was called away to a table of regulars, two men who ordered the same thing every week and argued about the sauce. While she was gone, Zoe flipped through her notebook and found an article Marceline had printed for her three weeks ago and that she had dismissed as babyish: a short piece about a bakery in Lyon that had stayed open for a hundred years. She started reading it silently, just to have something to do, and something strange happened. She understood it. Not every word, but nearly all of them, and the ones she didn't know she could guess from the sentences around them, which had never once happened with the rents article.

When Marceline came back, wiping her hands on her apron, Zoe pushed the bakery article across the table. "This one I can read," she said. "Why can I read this one and not that one? They're both French. They're both real newspapers."

Marceline sat down across from her, which she almost never did during a shift. She pulled both articles toward her and looked at them, one and then the other, like a jeweler weighing stones. "There's a number for this," she said. "A linguist, Paul Nation, he and his colleagues did research on it. Readers need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help." She tapped the bakery article. "This one, you know maybe ninety-eight percent. That one," and she tapped the rents article, "maybe eighty. It's not you. It's the percentage."

Zoe sat with that. She had been thinking of comprehension as a kind of virtue, something you earned by effort, and failure as evidence of insufficient effort. The idea that it was arithmetic felt almost like being let out of detention. She counted, out of curiosity, the unknown words in one paragraph of the bakery article: two out of sixty-something. Then she counted the same paragraph of the other: eleven. She showed Marceline the numbers, and Marceline shrugged, as if to say that she had been telling her this for weeks in other ways.

"But I need the hard one," Zoe said. "For the credit. The extra credit is only for a real article, and the teacher said the textbook one is, you know..." She didn't finish. She had been about to say something dismissive, and the dismissiveness suddenly embarrassed her, sitting there in a restaurant where the easy dish and the hard dish were both food.

Marceline smiled at the unfinished sentence. "So read the bakery one until it's easy. Then the next one, a little harder. The rents article will still exist next month." She stood, because a couple had come in and were waiting near the door with the particular patience of people who expect to be recognized. At the pass she turned back and said, "Summarize the bakery for me. In French. Tonight, before I cut the desserts. One minute."

Zoe worked fast. She read the article twice more, wrote three sentences in French with the dictionary closed, crossed one out, and when Marceline returned with a plate of madeleines the kitchen had sent out by mistake, Zoe gave her summary aloud. It was short and her accent slipped on "centenaire," but it was all true: the bakery was old, the neighborhood had changed, the baker's granddaughter kept it going because she had grown up above the ovens. Marceline listened with her arms folded, then nodded once, the way the regulars nodded when the sauce was right.

It was only later, packing up, that Zoe looked at the extra credit sheet again and saw the line she had skipped in her hurry to choose the difficult thing. The teacher had written: any authentic article, at your level, summarized aloud; difficulty of the text is not the criterion. The hard article and the bakery article were worth exactly the same points. Zoe laughed at herself, quietly, in the emptying restaurant, and put both articles in her bag anyway. She wasn't sure yet which one she would hand in, or whether she would try the rents article one more time first, on her own, with the dictionary, just to see if eighty percent had crept up toward ninety.

Marceline called goodnight from the door, and Zoe went out into the street with the taste of madeleine still on her tongue, the two articles folded together in her back pocket.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
Mrs. Bell's studio smelled of lemon polish and cold coffee, and the piano held its lid up like a pugnacious little animal baring its teeth. Juliette set her score of Mozart's K. 333 on the rack, already braced for the argument she had been rehearsing on the bus.

"You're ten minutes late," said Mrs. Bell, who was not actually annoyed, which they both knew, since she was already pouring tea.

"The bus was late, and I was composing my defense." Juliette flipped to the second movement and flattened the page with her palm. "I marked it. Exposition, development, recapitulation. Colors and everything. Green for the first theme, blue for the second, orange for the closing business. I used orange for anything that felt like closing business, which turned out to be a lot of things."

Mrs. Bell leaned over her shoulder without touching the score, a habit of hers that Juliette had never fully acclimated to, this hovering inspection, like a gull deciding whether your sandwich was worth the dive. "And where does your development end?"

"Page four, measure ninety-eight. Where the first theme comes back in the right hand." Juliette said it fast, the way you say the thing you are most sure of when you suspect you shouldn't be.

"Hm," said Mrs. Bell, which was the sound of a verdict being postponed, of acquittal denied on a technicality. "Play from measure eighty."

Juliette played. The music wandered, as developments do, through keys that felt like rooms in someone else's house, familiar furniture arranged wrong. Then, somewhere around measure ninety, the harmony settled and leaned, and leaned, and stayed leaning, and Juliette felt her own shoulders tilt forward at the keyboard, because the opening tune felt inches away, about to walk through the door.

She kept playing. And the tune did come back, in the left hand, in the wrong key, grinning at her like a prank.

"That," said Juliette, stopping, "is mean. That's a mean thing for Mozart to do."

"Play it again," Mrs. Bell said, and sipped her tea.

Juliette played it again, and this time she listened instead of expecting. The harmony before the tease had been sitting on the dominant of the home key, churning, the same chord, over and over, the whole passage refusing to move while insisting it was about to. That was the trick of it. The churning built the hunger, and Mozart fed her a lookalike first, in a key that was not home. Then, later, the real return arrived, the true one, in the tonic, green-pen territory at last. She reached over and moved her orange bracket.

"The churning part," she said slowly, penciling a bracket and the word retransition above it, because a thing that did that deserved a name and Mrs. Bell had refused to say it first, out of some teacher's code. "It's a retransition. It parks on the dominant and makes you think the first theme is coming home."

"I said nothing," said Mrs. Bell, hands raised, tea sloshing gently.

"You were thinking it very loudly." Juliette wrote a small note in the margin, near the lookalike theme: false alarm, he's teasing, wait for it. Then she sat back. "Okay, but here's what I can't decide. At the concert Friday, when Devin leaned forward at that same spot, I thought he was hearing the homecoming. But now I think he was hearing the tease. Or maybe there is no difference. Maybe the wanting is the point, and the trick is that you enjoy being fooled."

"You want my answer?"

"I want you to tell me I'm right and also wrong in an interesting way."

Mrs. Bell laughed, a short bark that rattled the teacups. "I'll tell you that Devin falls asleep in the slow movements and wakes up for exactly these moments, every concert, like a man whose body knows sonata form better than his mind does. Beyond that, you're on your own."

Juliette looked at the page, at the orange and green brackets now overlapping in one guilty measure, at the word retransition in her own cramped hand. She picked up the pencil, hovered, and wrote nothing.

"Next week," she said, "can we do the ones where he delays the second theme? Apparently I like being toyed with."

"Eighth notes, first thing, no warm-up," said Mrs. Bell, and turned back the pages to the beginning.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
Kaitlyn's mother ran the travel agency on Dufferin Street, and on the last Tuesday of August Kaitlyn sat at the empty second desk doing her summer packet for AP Human Geography. The assignment said: choose two countries, compare their population pyramids, and write a paragraph predicting what each would need more of in twenty years, schools or nursing homes. She had picked Japan first because it was easy. Then she flipped through the atlas her mother kept for the safari brochures and stopped on Niger.

The pyramid for Japan looked like a top spinning on a wide point: fat bars in the sixties and seventies, then narrowing to almost nothing at the base. The pyramid for Niger looked like a steep triangle, wide at the bottom, the whole shape leaning toward young. She counted the bars twice. The bottom ones, zero to four, four to nine, ran so far across the page that she had to check the scale against Japan's, sure there was a printing error. There was not.

"You've been quiet for an hour," her mother said from behind the counter, where she was fitting a client's itinerary into a folder. The client, a Mr. Osei, was going to Accra in September.

"Doing homework. Can I ask you something? You took that group to West Africa last spring, right?"

"Two groups. One to Senegal, one routed through Niger on the river circuit."

"Was there, like, a lot of kids? Little kids, I mean."

Mr. Osei turned around while his card was running. "Half the country is children," he said. "I'm from Ghana, next door, and even we say Niger is young. Highest birth rate in the world, more or less. You go to the market there and it's children selling to children." He signed the slip, took his folder, and said the riparian lodges had been overbooked both weeks, everyone wanting the rooms on the riverbank, and then he left.

Kaitlyn drew the shape again in her notebook. If such a large share of the population were children, and the base were that wide, then in twenty years those children would have children, or would be teaching them. She had been treating the pyramid as a picture of the past, a record of who was already born, but Mr. Osei's market full of children made it forward-facing, a forecast. Japan needed nursing homes. Niger needed schools, classrooms, teachers, desks, all of it at a scale she could not get from the flat page. She wrote: a very wide base and a large share of children means the demand for schooling will keep compounding, and then crossed out "compounding" because she could not prove that, only the shape.

Her mother came over and looked at the two pyramids. "Which one's the problem?"

"Neither. That's the thing. My draft says Japan has a problem and Niger doesn't, and I don't believe that's what the data says. Niger has to build for all those kids starting basically now. I just can't tell whether that's a problem or just a fact."

"Then say that."

"I can't. The rubric wants a prediction."

Her mother went back to the phone, where a client wanted to know whether the river cruise included the floodplain villages, the ones strung out along the water. Kaitlyn tried a different approach. She looked up the etymology of "demography," writing the people, description, in the margin because Ms. Ferrante gave a point for word histories, and found that it did not help her decide anything. It only reminded her that the whole science had started with someone counting births and deaths in parishes, one clerk, one register, no better positioned than she was now.

She remembered, also, that she had told a girl at orientation that geography was the slacker AP. The memory did not exculpate her now, sitting with a question she could not close. She could state the fact cleanly: Niger had one of the highest birth rates in the world, its pyramid had a very wide base, a large share of its people were children. From that, schools, not nursing homes. What she could not state was whether the schools would come, or whether the pyramid's shape alone told you anything about what a country would choose to do about its own future.

She typed the paragraph twice and deleted the second version, which had drift toward certainty. In the final draft she wrote the prediction and then one sentence after it: the pyramid shows who exists, not what happens next. She read it over and decided it was honest rather than evasive, which was the argument she would make if Ferrante pushed back, and she knew Ferrante would.

The printer by the brochure rack was out of toner. Kaitlyn saved the file, closed the atlas on Niger, and stood it back on the shelf between Iceland and Oman, spine out, the triangle of children hidden inside.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
story:
Rose found the video at 7:14 in the morning, propped against the lockers outside the science wing while she waited for first bell. A bridge buckling, a reporter's voice cracking, a caption in bold letters: HAPPENING NOW. Sixty thousand shares already. Her thumb hovered over the send button, because Priya would want to see it before anyone else did, and being first had always been their currency.

Then Marcus leaned over her shoulder, chewing the end of a pen. "That's not now," he said. "That's old. I've seen it before."

"You've seen everything before. You live online."

"I'm serious." He pulled out his phone, thumbs moving fast. "You can check. TinEye, it's called. You put the picture in and it finds where it's been." He tilted the screen toward her. "It's been around since 2008, so it catches a lot."

The first bell rang down the hall and neither of them moved. Marcus tapped a sorting option. "Oldest first," he said. "You want the oldest one, that's where it started."

The results loaded and the top of the list showed a date four years old. Not a similar bridge, the same bridge, same angle, same gray water underneath. The caption on the original page was in another language and the page itself had gone quiet years ago, comments trailing off mid-argument, the way conversations do when everyone simply drifts.

Rose sent Priya a different message instead: check before you forward that bridge thing. Then she stood there feeling oddly foolish, because she had been certain, absolutely certain, and the certainty had been worth nothing. In third period, half-listening to Mr. Okafor define indemnity as a security against loss, a word that slid past her because she was still thinking about the bridge, she copied the term into her notes anyway. Something about the word stayed with her. A check was a kind of security, she thought. Not against money lost, but against something else being spent.

At lunch Priya slid her tray across from Rose's, phone already out. "I almost sent it to my whole group chat," she said. "My aunt did. Half my family did. So what, though? It's still a real bridge. It still fell somewhere."

"It fell four years ago." Rose turned her phone around. "Look. Marcus showed me this thing. Reverse image search. You can sort it oldest first and see when it first appeared." She watched Priya's face do what her own had done that morning: the small collapse of certainty, followed quickly by a defense. "It's a real disaster," Priya said. "People should care about it anyway."

"People should care about it as what it is," Rose said, and heard how preachy it sounded, and kept going anyway. "If we share it as now, then next week, when something is actually happening, who believes us?" She thought of the way the whole feed could desensitize you, one crying wolf after another until a real wolf arrived and everyone scrolled past. She didn't say that part out loud. Priya was already scrolling, thumb slow now, actually reading.

The problem, Rose admitted to herself on the walk to fifth period, was that she hadn't fully worked out what she believed. The video was manipulative, sure. But Priya had a point too: the bridge had fallen, people had died, and the world's attention was a scarce thing that old lies were stealing from new truths. Maybe sometimes an old image found new eyes that needed to see it. She didn't know where the line was. She knew only that she had almost drawn one in permanent ink and Marcus had handed her an eraser.

After school she sat on the wall by the auxiliary gym, the one nobody used since the main gym was rebuilt, and did it herself this time, start to finish. Her own photo of a flooded street she'd shared in September, the one that had made her feel so urgent and useful. Oldest first: two years, three months. She stared at it while the buses idled in the lot below.

Priya sat down beside her with a bag of chips and looked at the screen. "Yours too?"

"Mine too." Rose locked the phone and watched a freshman chase a rolling water bottle across the blacktop. "Delete it or leave it?"

"Leave it," Priya said. "But write the real date. Show people how you know."

Rose unlocked the phone and started typing.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Lucas had been told to watch the table while his aunt fetched change from the van, and in the four minutes she was gone he sold three bars of chocolate and one jar of honey, which was more than she usually sold in an hour. The market smelled of bread and cut peonies. He kept one eye on the customers and one on the thermometer clipped to the steel bowl, where the milk chocolate sat at 31.5 degrees and refused to do anything but sit there, dull and soft, refusing to set on the test spoon the way it had set every Saturday since April.

He had made the batch himself, before dawn, in the church kitchen his aunt rented. Tempering was the word she used, and her maxim, delivered while seeding the bowl with chopped chocolate, was that tempering was patience made edible: heat it, cool it, hold it, and the chocolate would come out shiny and snap when you broke it. He had watched her do it for dark chocolate a dozen times, holding the bowl at about 32 degrees, and that morning he had simply done what he had watched her do.

The result was on the table in front of him: sixty truffle shells with surfaces like fogged windows, tacky to the touch of a knife, no snap at all. He had a customer coming at eleven who wanted two hundred shells for a wedding, and it was ten. His aunt, Marguerite, came back counting fives, looked at the test spoon, and pressed her thumb into one shell.

"You ran it hot," she said. Not accusing, just reporting.

"Thirty-two. Same as the dark, the whole way through."

She turned the spoon over. "That's your trouble, then. Dark takes thirty-two. Milk chocolate is tempered lower, twenty-nine to thirty. I thought I told you."

"You told me milk was easier."

"I did say that." She was already pulling the失败的 batch toward the edge of the table, then stopped herself and looked at him instead of at the chocolate. "I told you milk was easier and you heard that you didn't have to listen. Fix it. You've got the wedding order and I've got the stall."

He did not say anything back. He carried the bowl to the van, where the portable burner and the seed chocolate lived, and rewarmed the batch to melt it out completely, then cooled it, stirring, adding a handful of chopped chocolate a few pieces at a time. His phone showed 29.4 degrees when he stopped adding and let the thermometer settle. At home he would have looked it up, cross-checked it, probably found some forum argument about whether the lower temperature mattered or whether people were being superstitious about it. In the van doorway with a wedding order ninety minutes away, he had only the number Marguerite had given him and the spoon.

He dipped the spoon and set it on the cold steel counter of the van. Nothing happened that he could see. He wiped his hands and waited, and the customer arrived early, a woman in a rain jacket who wanted to taste the milk before committing to two hundred shells, and Lucas had to walk back to the stall and slice the one good bar from last week and talk about cocoa percentages while his eyes kept drifting toward the van.

Marguerite found him mid-sentence. She held up the spoon without a word. The chocolate on it had gone hard and smooth, and when she snapped it against the counter it broke clean, with a sound like a small dry branch.

"Milk fat," she said. "It softens the cocoa butter, so the milk wants it cooler. Twenty-nine, thirty." She handed him the spoon as if it were a certificate. "Now the shells."

He worked through the noon rush sideways, dipping and setting shells on a marble slab in the shade of the van, checking the thermometer more often than he needed to because he did not entirely trust a number he had learned from a sentence. It held, though. It held at 29.6, and then 30.1 when the sun came out, and he stirred and cooled it back down without panic. He still did not know whether the fault had been his listening or her telling, and he suspected the answer was both and would stay both, the way most answers in their kitchen did.

The wedding customer came back at one and bought the two hundred, running her thumb along one shell's shine. Behind the table, Lucas bagged them and said, "Careful with the back seat, they're firm now but heat is heat." She laughed, paid, and carried the boxes off between the flower stalls, and he turned the thermometer so he could read it from where he stood.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
story:
Eva found the bug in fourth period, though it was not really a bug. Marcus had written a program to look up student names in the attendance file, a list of two thousand names in alphabetical order, and it ran in an instant whenever the name was there. But when he typed in a name that was not in the file, the cursor just sat there, spinning, while the rest of the class moved on to the next exercise.

"Maybe the network's slow," Marcus said, but the boy across the aisle had no trouble with his own program. Eva leaned over. She read his loop, one line at a time, and saw what it did: it started at the first name and checked each one against the target, moving down the list item by item. When the name existed, the loop could stop early, somewhere in the middle. When the name did not exist, there was nothing to stop it. The loop had to go all the way to the end, checking every single name, before it could say the person wasn't there.

"It's not the network," she said quietly, so Ms. Rojas wouldn't hear. "It's your search. Look. You start at the beginning and check one by one. That's called a linear search. If the name is last on the list, or if it isn't there at all, you have to look at every item." Marcus frowned at his screen, then at the ceiling, then back. "Every item," he repeated. "Two thousand names." "Two thousand names," Eva said, "for one absent person."

Ms. Rojas called the class together before the bell and wrote two words on the board: binary search. She would not explain it, she said, because they were going to build it themselves, and she handed out a exercise sheet with a printed list of sorted names and a set of questions. Sorted was underlined twice. Eva read the first question. Why does the list have to be in order?

She thought about it while everyone around her started scribbling. Her mother, who taught philosophy at the community college, had a habit of asking what a thing assumes. Binary search, whatever it was, seemed to assume order, the way a dictionary assumed the alphabet. You couldn't look up "cosmopolitan" in a dictionary with shuffled pages; the alphabetical arrangement was the whole reason you could leap to the C section instead of starting at page one. That was it, she thought. The sorted list carried information about where things weren't.

At lunch, Marcus sat with his laptop in the courtyard, still wounded from fourth period. "I felt like an idiot," he said. "Everyone's program answered in a blink and mine just hung there." Eva tore her sandwich in half and pushed the larger piece across the table without commenting on it, which was how they did things. "You weren't wrong," she said. "Your logic was fine. You just picked the slow tool. Nobody's going to pathologize you for one bad loop." He laughed a little at that, and she took the printed list from her bag and laid it flat between their trays.

She put her finger on the middle name. "The list is sorted, so the middle tells you something. If the target comes after this name alphabetically, everything above it is ruled out. Half the list, gone, in one check." She moved her finger to the middle of what remained, then the middle of what remained after that, and Marcus watched her hand the way people watch a card trick. "So with your linear search, the worst case, the name last or missing, means checking every item. With this, the worst case is a handful of checks, because you throw away half each time." She was not certain her program would work; she had not written a line of it yet, and she said so. "I think that's the idea. I could still be wrong about the details."

They wrote it together after school in the lab that smelled faintly of whiteboard marker, Marcus typing and Eva narrating, then switching, then arguing about whether the comparison should use the middle element or the one just past it, and finding a wrong answer once, then finding it again, and then, at 4:40, watching the cursor blink and return a verdict in less time than it took to see it happen. Marcus typed a name that was not in the file. The answer came instantly. He typed another, a real one, the last name on the list, and it came just as fast, and he sat back in the plastic chair with his hands laced behind his head.

"It's almost unfair," he said. "The old program did all that work for nothing." Eva closed her notebook. Outside the window, Ms. Rojas was locking the door of the classroom across the hall, and the parking lot beyond her was already half empty. "It's like the difference between reading every page and using the index," Eva said. "Or between a country where everyone's equal and a plutocracy, where the money's all sorted to the top, so you only have to look in one place to find it." Marcus looked at her. "Did you just compare my attendance program to government corruption?" "Sorted data," Eva said, "is political." She picked up her bag, and they walked out together into the cold.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
story:
Sebastian had told his father, with the confidence of a boy who had watched four YouTube tutorials, that their street was perfectly safe from flooding, and his father had replied, "Then why did the insurance letter say otherwise," and that was how the whole argument began, a Saturday-morning dispute conducted over toast about whether the man from the insurance company was a swindler or a messenger. Sebastian decided to settle it with data, because data, unlike his father, could not raise its voice. He carried his laptop to the kitchen table, opened the GIS software he was learning for his community college summer course, and began layering the city map: flood risk polygons on the bottom, housing parcels on top, his own neighborhood a scatter of beige rectangles along Ridgeview Avenue, which, despite its promising name, sat a full mile from the river.

"That's the point," Sebastian said aloud, to no one. "A mile. Water doesn't walk uphill for a mile to ruin Dad's lawnmower."

His sister Priya wandered in, eating cereal directly from the box like a pelagic fish cruising the open ocean, mouth open, always moving, and leaned over his shoulder. She was home from her first year of college and considered it her duty to question everything he did. "What are you doing?"

"Winning an argument."

"Against who?"

"Dad. And geography."

The flood risk layer, when he turned it on, painted the river's banks an obvious and satisfying blue, which he expected. What he did not expect was a second blue blotch, fat and irregular, sitting directly over the eastern half of Ridgeview, nowhere near any water at all. Streets a mile from the river showed risk. He toggled the layer off and on, as though the software might admit it had made a mistake, or as though he could embarrass it into honesty. The blotch stayed. Priya crunched her cereal above him like distant thunder.

"There's no river there," Sebastian said. "There's not even a creek. There's a Costco."

"Maybe water just really likes bulk shopping," Priya offered, and he would have laughed if the blotch had not included, when he overlaid the housing parcels, a beige rectangle that was recognizably, unmistakably, his own house.

He sat back. His father drifted in for more coffee, saw the screen, and said nothing, which was somehow louder than the earlier shouting. Sebastian stared at the blue stain over Ridgeview and tried to think of it as a mistake, a clerical ghost, but the software's data came from the city, and the city had no reason to lie about a neighborhood it barely remembered existed. He opened the layer list looking for something, anything, that would explain it, and found a file he had skipped past earlier: the digital elevation model. He remembered his instructor saying it once, quickly, in passing. "A digital elevation model," she had said, "is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell," and he had written it down and then, in the tradition of students everywhere, ignored his own notes. Now he clicked it on, and the map changed color entirely, a wash of greens and browns and one deep, sulky purple.

The purple was a bowl. He could see it plainly once the elevation layer was up: Ridgeview sat lower than everything around it, a shallow dish of ground tucked behind the ridge the street was named for, and the river, when it rose, was not the only actor. Water fell everywhere, on every roof and parking lot, and gravity, indifferent to distance and to Sebastian's argument with his father, moved it all downhill into the bowl. The flood model wasn't tracking the river. It was tracking where water would flow and collect, cell by cell, and the cells of Ridgeview were, apparently, a destination. The Costco, he noted with grim satisfaction, sat comfortably up on the green.

"So you were wrong," Priya said, reading the map over his shoulder with the tact of a gull.

"I wasn't wrong. I was incomplete. There's a difference, and it's the difference between science and, like, Dad."

His father set his coffee down and pulled out the chair beside him, which was itself a small miracle, a rapprochement conducted entirely in furniture. "Show me the part where you were incomplete," he said, and there was no smugness in it, which made it worse, or better, Sebastian couldn't decide. He walked his father through it, clicking layers on and off: the flood polygons, the parcels, the elevation model glowing purple under their house like a bruise the ground had been hiding. His father asked one question, then another, then said, quietly, "So the insurance man wasn't lying." Sebastian said no. His father said, "Huh," and drank his coffee, and after a moment he asked whether the software could show the map for Priya's college town, because her landlord had been saying the basement was dry as a bone, and Priya said, "Absolutely not," and reached for the laptop.

Sebastian got there first. "One condition," he said, already zooming out, already hunting for the layer list. "When it turns out her basement's a swimming pool, I get to say so at dinner."

"Deal," said his father, before Priya could object, and slid his chair closer to the screen.

Mackenzie spread the returned quiz on the library table and looked at it the way you look at a tooth that aches when you press it. Four marks gone, and beside her answer the teacher had written only "see me," which she had not done, because seeing him meant admitting she still didn't understand something she was supposed to have understood in October. Her answer was right in every part except one. At the end of it, after she had evaluated at the upper limit and subtracted what she got at the lower limit, she had written plus C, and he had circled it twice in red.

The library at four o'clock was mostly empty, the light through the tall windows going long and amber across the carpet. Priya arrived with two binders and a granola bar and dropped into the chair across from her, already talking about the debate tournament, which she was desperate to make varsity for. "I need the syllabus points," she said, snapping a binder open. "They weight the speaking events, and I keep getting picked for interpretive, which nobody cares about. If I can't get policy, I'm going to quit, I swear." She said this every week, and every week she came back with two binders.

Mackenzie turned the quiz so Priya could see it, though Priya was still reading her own notes. "Why is it wrong," she said. "The C, I mean. Why is it wrong to put the C there?"

"You did that on the homework too," Priya said, not looking up. "I just erased it for you."

"You erased it?"

"Mrs. Trujillo circled mine the first time and Priya fixed it after," Priya said. "I figured it was a rule. Like not wearing white after Labor Day. You just don't do it."

That was the part that bothered Mackenzie, and she knew it bothered her in a way that was slightly unreasonable, the way certain small injustices do. She didn't want it to be a rule, an etiquette. She wanted it to be a reason. She had grown up around rules that were only rules, her mother's, mostly, and had developed a private loyalty to the idea that underneath most things there was something you could actually follow, some structure that would hold your weight. Priya called this her rationalism, half teasing, the same way she called Mackenzie's taste in music melancholic, and both words had stuck.

So she pulled a fresh sheet of paper and started over, slowly, writing out the antiderivative with C beside it like a passenger she wasn't sure she was allowed to bring. She evaluated it at the upper limit, and then at the lower limit, and then she sat very still, because something had happened on the page that she hadn't expected to be able to see. She wrote it out a second time to be sure. Then she underlined nothing, because there was nothing to underline, and that was the point.

"Look," she said, and turned the sheet around. Priya looked, chewing the last of the granola bar. At the top of the page, in Mackenzie's small, even handwriting, was the constant of integration sitting beside the antiderivative. At the upper limit, F of b plus C. At the lower limit, F of a plus C. And then the subtraction line, where she had written them one under the other, and where the C had appeared twice, once in each, before being subtracted away. It was simply gone, and not gone because someone had erased it. Gone because both of them had it.

"So it cancels," Priya said. "It cancels before you even get to the answer."

"It was never going to survive," Mackenzie said. "You add it twice and then you subtract, and it takes itself out. It doesn't matter which C it even is." She felt something she was embarrassed by, a small real gladness, as if she had been trusted with something. All year she had been bracing herself against this class, letting the repeated small failures desensitize her to the larger ones, and here was one failure that turned out, when she finally looked straight at it, to have a shape.

Priya was already back in her binder, running a highlighter down a column of debate evidence. "That's like my plan," she said. "Trujillo said a good closing is one where everything you set up at the start gets taken back at the end." She looked up, her pen hovering. "Do you think I should just email the coach and ask for policy directly? Or is that too much?" Outside, the amber light had slid off the carpet and onto the shelf of old atlases, and Mackenzie, still holding the sheet with the vanished C, said, "Email him tonight. Before you talk yourself out of it."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
story:
The microfilm room smelled of warm dust and machine oil, and Landon had been turning the crank of the reader for forty minutes before he found anything worth copying. His assignment sheet, folded into quarters on the table, asked for a historiographical essay: not what happened in the French Revolution, but how people had written about it since 1800, and why the writing kept changing. He had understood the assignment in the way you understand a word you cannot yet use, and now he was hunting through the library's old shelves for something primary enough to count. His friend Dex sat two seats away, ostensibly studying for a chemistry final, actually watching a girl at the copy machine.

"Find your old dead guy yet?" Dex said without looking up.

"Working on it." Landon had a stack of books beside him, and on top of them a battered volume he'd pulled because the name on the spine sounded vaguely familiar. Adolphe Thiers. He had opened it at random and struck a passage praising Mirabeau's steadiness, then turned a page and found Robespierre described in terms usually reserved for plague ships.

The girl at the copy machine walked past their table on her way out, and Dex watched her go with the patient attention of a birdwatcher. "She's in my calc class," he said. "Virtuoso with the integrals. Terrifying."

"Mm." Landon was not listening. He was reading the preface, and the preface was doing something strange to his assumptions. He had walked in that afternoon with a simple plan: the revolution had heroes and villains, and historians mostly disagreed about which were which, and his essay would line them up like a bracket. Marxists on one side, romantics on the other, neat as a debate he could referee. But Thiers was not lining up. Thiers liked Mirabeau and Lafayette, the moderates, the ones who tried to slow things down, and he could not stand the radicals. Fine, Landon thought, one vote for the moderates. Except the book had been published between 1823 and 1827, which meant Thiers had written it while the revolution was still a living memory, while its survivors were still arguing in Paris cafés, and that changed what the praise was for. It was not analysis from a distance. It was a man taking sides in a fight that had never ended.

He copied the publication dates onto his notecard, then sat back. The chair's plastic creaked in the silent room. Down the row, an older man was reading a newspaper with a truculent set to his jaw, turning pages hard, as if each one had personally disappointed him.

"So he liked the moderates," Landon said quietly to Dex. "Mirabeau, Lafayette. Condemned Robespierre. That's the whole judgment, right there, in three volumes."

"Who's Mirabeau?"

"A guy who tried to keep the king and the revolution talking to each other." Landon tapped the book. "But here's the thing. Thiers wrote this before he ever ran France himself. He wrote the history first, then went and made history after. So is the book about the revolution, or about what Thiers wanted France to be while he was writing it?"

Dex considered this with the seriousness he usually reserved for lunch. "Both, probably."

"Both is not an essay," Landon said, though even as he said it he suspected both was the truth. He tried anyway. For an hour he built the bracket: Thiers and the moderates versus later historians who redeemed the radicals, and the essay would trace the pendulum, swing by swing, as though each generation simply chose a new favorite. It was clean. It would have been easy. And at the center of it, like a stone in his shoe, sat the fact that would not flatten out: Thiers had not been choosing a favorite. He had been writing from inside the question, a citizen of the country whose revolution he was judging, with something at stake in the answer. The bracket assumed the historians were standing outside the painting pointing at it. Thiers was in the painting.

He tore up the outline he'd drafted, which stung, because it had been good, the kind of thing that would have earned a tidy checkmark at the top of the page. Instead he started a new notecard: how does where a historian stands change what they see, and can you ever stand nowhere. He wrote the question and then, underneath it, honest as he could bear to be, I don't know yet.

The lights dimmed for the closing announcement. Dex stacked his chemistry book, having studied nothing. "You figure out your dead guy?"

"He's not dead in the right way," Landon said. "He's still alive in the argument. That's the problem."

"That sounds like a C to me."

"It might be." Landon slid the Thiers volume into the return cart, and his fingers lingered on the cover a second, the way you touch a thing you are not done with. At the door, Dex held it open for the girl from calc, who had come back for a forgotten umbrella, and the three of them stepped out together into the cold blue end of the afternoon, Landon still holding his notecard with the unanswered question faceup in his hand.

story:
Benjamin had promised his geography teacher a project he was starting to regret: a map of the city showing which neighborhoods sat in the official flood zone, and which sat near it without technically being in it. The distinction had seemed like a footnote when he'd proposed it. Now, on the third night of summer, he sat at the kitchen table with his mother's laptop, a bowl of untouched cereal beside him, clicking through layers of public data he had spent two days learning to collate into something readable.

The software was mercurial, cooperative one minute and sulking the next. He'd gotten the parcels layer to load, each property in the city a small polygon, and then the flood layer, a pale blue wash that followed the river through the eastern neighborhoods like a stain. Where the two overlapped, the map turned a confident teal. Where they didn't, it stayed stubbornly ordinary, and that was the problem. He knew, from a summer of delivering groceries down by Felton Street, that water did not read maps.

His younger sister Nadia drifted through for a glass of milk and stopped behind his shoulder, which she did whenever she wanted something but hadn't decided what yet.

"What's the blue?"

"Flood zone. Where the city says it floods."

"And the other colors?"

"That's what I can't figure out how to show." He rotated the trackball, thinking out loud more than explaining. "There's a tool that draws a zone of a set distance around a feature. Like, every area within 100 meters of the river. It's called a buffer."

"Sounds like something you buy at a hardware store."

"It kind of is." He opened the analysis menu, found the tool, and typed 100 into the distance field, hoping he was choosing meters and not the other unit, whose name he had decided not to think about until the map proved him wrong.

The buffer bloomed around the river in a wide yellow band, wider than the flood zone, swallowing it and then some, reaching into blocks the blue had never touched. He clipped it against the parcels layer, and suddenly hundreds of homes that sat outside the official flood zone appeared inside the buffer, including, when he zoomed to Felton Street, a whole row of porches he recognized. The Tavares house was in the yellow. The blue stopped two doors down.

Then, because he was thorough in the way of someone avoiding the harder question of what the map meant, he searched his own address.

The pushpin dropped into the yellow band. Not the blue. Their house, the one his mother had spent four years saving toward because it was outside the flood zone and therefore, the realtor had said, "a smart buy," sat inside every area within 100 meters of the river. He sat back. The cereal had gone soft in its milk, and he ate it anyway, slowly, watching the pushpin as though it might reconsider.

His mother came home at nine with a bag of groceries and the particular tiredness of someone who had been on her feet since seven. He almost closed the laptop. Instead he turned it toward her when she set the bags down.

"Is that the project? Looks nice."

"It's the river." He pointed at the yellow. "This part is every area within 100 meters of it. The flood zone's smaller. We're in the yellow part, not the blue."

She looked at the screen for a long moment, then at him, then back at the screen. "We don't flood. Mrs. Okafor's yard took on water in the spring and ours didn't."

"I know. That's what the data says too, sort of. The blue is where it's actually flooded." He moved the cursor along the band. "But look how many houses are in the yellow and not the blue. There's no category for them. They're not in the flood zone, so nothing applies to them. They're just near it."

She started unpacking the groceries, more slowly than usual. "The realtor said outside the flood zone. That was true, wasn't it?"

"It was true."

She set a carton of eggs in the refrigerator door with unusual care. He understood, then, that he had handed her something she would carry to work tomorrow and turn over during her lunch break, and that he could not take it back by telling her the flood data was eleven years old, or that buffers were a blunt instrument, or that a hundred meters was a number someone had chosen for convenience. All of that was true too. He had checked the veracity of every layer he'd downloaded, and still the honest map was the one that said: probably fine, and near.

"You should put a legend on that," his mother said, closing the refrigerator. "Yellow means what, exactly?"

"That's the thing," Benjamin said. "I don't have a word for it yet."

Nadia, who had been listening from the doorway with the empty milk glass still in her hand, said, "Call it the almost."

story:
Elliot had taken the job at the Saturday market because it was close to campus and the pay was cash, but by his third weekend he understood that his real duties were lifting, apologizing, and standing between two stallholders who loved each other and could not agree on anything. Mr. Addo sold honey from hives up the hill. Priya sold apples, cider, and, in October, doughnuts whose smell seemed to sequester half the crowd at one end of the lot. Every Saturday at ten, when the rush thinned, Priya walked a basket of apples to Mr. Addo and tried to leave with jars of honey, and every Saturday the argument began again.

"You gave me three jars last time," Priya said, setting the basket on the counter of the honey stall.

"Four. And the apples were small." Mr. Addo held one up to the light as if it might confess. Elliot, restocking jars behind them, kept his head down and his ears open, which was, he had discovered, the position from which he learned the most at this job. He was eighteen and had just started economics, and he had been staring all week at a diagram in his textbook, two curved lines, a sentence about gains from trade, and a feeling in his chest like a door not quite shut.

The argument had a shape, he noticed, the way an argument in a family has a shape. Priya would say that her apples took all season and his honey took all summer, so even was even. Mr. Addo would say that she was counting seasons and he was counting days, that a hive needed tending every single day, and that she spent her time pressing cider too, which he did not do at all. Neither of them ever said what a basket of apples cost them, each in the other's good. They said what things were worth, which was different, and the difference was exactly the thing Elliot's professor kept circling without naming.

"Ten forty-five," Priya said, glancing at the clock on the church across the road. "The wholesaler comes at eleven and I need those jars before he sees me buying at retail." The wholesaler was a large man named Victor who arrived each Saturday at eleven sharp to buy whatever Priya hadn't sold, and Priya hated, more than rain or wasps, for Victor to see her trading with a neighbor, because Victor believed hedonism was the only sensible business model and said so loudly. Eleven o'clock was their deadline, and they both knew it.

It was Mr. Addo, that morning, who finally said the sentence that moved the argument sideways. "You want to talk economics with your first-year head," he said to Elliot, catching him listening. "Tell her what she is really asking me for." And Elliot, put on the spot with the clock already leaning toward eleven, found that the diagram in his textbook had quietly become a thing he could hold up.

"The thing we learned is called comparative advantage," he said, wiping his hands on his apron. "But that's not the part that settles this. The part is the price." He looked from one of them to the other. "You both only gain if the trade lands somewhere between what it costs you, Priya, to make honey yourself, if you gave up apples to do it, and what it costs you, Mr. Addo, to make apples yourself, if you gave up honey to do it. Somewhere between those two. That's the whole fair range."

From where Priya stood, basket on her hip, the boy's voice had a strange steadiness, and she did the arithmetic she had never once done in fifteen years of Saturdays. If she wanted to keep bees, she would have to give up a row of trees, and the trees were her living, so honey would cost her dearly. If Mr. Addo wanted to grow apples, he would have to give up half his hive sites to make room, and his honey was his living, so apples would cost him dearly too. Each of them was cheap in their own good and ruinously expensive in the other's, which meant there was a wide stretch of prices where a trade would leave both of them better off, and a narrow stretch outside it where one of them would be quietly losing.

"Five jars," she said, "and I throw in the doughnuts I can't sell today, because they're evanescent, they're gone by Sunday, and you like them."

"Four jars," said Mr. Addo, "and the doughnuts, and you admit the last basket was small."

Victor's van was already turning into the lot, its grill catching the sun. Priya looked at the jars, at the doughnut box sweating grease through its lid, at the church clock, and put out her hand. "Four and the doughnuts," she said, "and next week we settle the range before I walk over, so this doesn't take till Christmas."

Mr. Addo shook it, and slid the doughnut box toward himself with his free hand, already open.

story:
Justine had written and deleted the message eleven times, and the twelfth draft still read like something a hostage would send. She sat on the sunporch of her grandparents' house with her phone balanced on her knee, the screen door banging behind her in the warm June wind, trying once more to figure out how to tell Priya that she had missed practice twice in the week before sectionals.

The trouble was that Justine knew exactly how not to do it. Last spring she had told Marta, after a dropped relay handoff, "You always mess up when it counts," and Marta had quit the relay entirely, and Justine had spent the summer understanding that she had not been wrong about the handoff, only about everything else. She wanted to say the true thing to Priya without becoming that girl again, the one whose honesty arrived like weather, flattening whatever it touched.

From the kitchen came her grandfather's voice, querulous and rising: "I put the flag out at seven, Dorothy, not nine. Seven. I have not once forgotten the flag since Carter." There was a pause, and then her grandmother said, with the calm of a woman holding all the cards, "I asked about the lawnmower, Frank, not the flag." Her grandfather muttered something about how she changed the subject like a populist changes the topic, whatever that meant, and retreated to his armchair with a book.

Justine drifted in for a glass of water and saw the book's cover, something about marriage and relationships, with a serious-looking psychologist's name on the spine. Her grandfather held it at arm's length, mouthing the words. She was halfway back to the porch when he read a line aloud to himself, not to her, the way old men read when they think nobody is listening: "A complaint addresses a specific behavior, but criticism attacks the person's character." He nodded slowly, as though the sentence had personally accused him of something.

Justine stood in the doorway with her water. A complaint addresses a specific behavior. She turned it over. When she had said "you always mess up," she had not addressed the dropped baton at all; she had gone after Marta herself, the whole person, always and everywhere. Whereas "you missed practice twice" was only a fact with edges, a thing a person could actually pick up and look at. She did not know if it was true that one kind of sentence saved relationships and the other one broke them, and she supposed the book had studies for that, but what she knew for certain was that Marta had heard the second kind of sentence as the first kind, had heard you always when Justine had only meant that baton, that day.

She tried the drafts again on the porch, out loud now, because her grandmother had come out to deadhead the roses. "Priya, you missed practice twice this week, and we need to fix your start before Saturday." She said it twice, testing the weight of it. "That's better," she said, mostly to herself. "That's a thing she can do something about."

Her grandmother pinched off a spent bloom and dropped it in her apron pocket. "Your grandfather's been reading that book out loud for three weeks," she said. "Last night he informed me that when I say he never listens, that's criticism." She straightened, brushing dirt from her hands. "So this morning I said, Frank, you didn't hear a word I said about the gutters on Tuesday. He looked so pleased with himself for being lectured properly." She went inside, and Justine laughed alone on the porch, then wrote the message and sent it before she could draft a thirteenth version: You missed practice twice this week and I should have said something sooner instead of getting weird about it. Your start is the fastest on the team when you're there. Can we fix the second exchange before Saturday?

Priya's reply came in two minutes, which meant she had been staring at her phone too: I thought you were mad at me. My dad had his surgery Tuesday, I was at the hospital, I didn't know how to tell anyone. I'll be at the river field at six.

The twist, Justine thought, was that she had spent four days constructing a speech for someone who mostly needed to be asked. On Saturday Justine's mother drove her to the meet, stopping first at the bakery so Justine could buy the lemon cake Priya liked, partly to propitiate her for the four days of silence and partly because it was simply true that Priya liked lemon cake, and true things, she was learning, came in more than one kind.

At the river field that evening, Priya's start was still the fastest on the team, and the exchange they drilled eleven times was clean on the ninth, and Priya said, "See, this is why I wanted you to say something. You're the only one who notices stuff and then hoards it like a dragon." Justine lined up at the mark again, crouched, and called back over her shoulder, "On your go, and if I false start, say the baton, not my whole character."
