story:
The gymnasium smelled like rubber mats and solder, and the overhead fluorescents gave everyone a faintly jaundiced cast that Makayla had stopped noticing by ten in the morning. She sat behind the pit table with the team laptop open, the robot beside her with its side panel off, waiting for the semifinal round in ninety minutes. The problem was not mechanical. At the top of their code, a variable that every part of the program reached into directly had quietly become wrong.

Theo had rewritten it the night before, in the hotel room, because the gyro sensor was returning angles with decimals now. He had changed the field from a whole-number type to one that held decimal values, and when Makayla opened the file she expected disaster. She scrolled down through the arm code, the drive code, the autonomous routine, looking for the place where everything would break. Nothing broke. Every piece still compiled, still ran, and she sat with her hand on the trackpad, suspicious of her own relief.

"How," she said. Theo was across the table re-crimping a connector, and he shrugged without looking up.

"Everything goes through the getters," he said. "I changed how it stores the data and nothing else cared."

Makayla read the class again from the top. The fields were marked private, tucked away where no other file could touch them, and the only way in or out was through small public methods that handed back a value. "So nobody reaches in and grabs it directly," she said slowly. "They ask, and the class decides what to give them."

"That's the point of it," Theo said. "Hiding the data behind methods, so the rest of the code can use the object without depending on how it stores it." He tested the connector against the light. "It's called encapsulation. You can look it up, but that's basically it." He said it the way he said most things, flat and quick, as if facts were screws to be handed over one at a time, and then he went back to the crimping tool. Makayla wrote the word in the margin of her notebook and underlined it once, not twice, because twice felt like something she would be embarrassed by later.

She had always coded the other way, fields wide open, everything public, because that was what the tutorials showed and because it was faster, and speed had mattered more than tidiness when the robot was a shoebox with wheels. But the shoebox had become a competition machine, and last month, in the quarterfinals, a single rogue line of arm code had overwritten a heading value and sent the robot into the field wall. At the time she had blamed the sensor. Sitting here now, she understood it had been the reaching-in.

"Can you revert it?" she asked Theo, half hoping he would demur, and he did, shaking his head. "The decimals are right," he said. "The gyro's better this way. I'm not going back." His own want was plain enough: he had spent months on that sensor and he was not going to be the one to undo it. She could argue, or she could build.

So she built. She made a new class, a small one, with the heading and the arm position as private fields, with getters for each, and then, because she did not entirely trust her own reasoning yet, she wrote a test. She fed the class a value, asked for it back through the getter, and checked that what came out matched what went in. She ran it once and it passed, and she ran it again after changing the field's type, and it still passed, and she sat looking at the green bar in the test window feeling something settle that she could not yet have explained to anyone. Then she wired the drive code to ask instead of grab, method by method, deleting the reaching-in as she went, while Theo watched sideways and the loudspeaker called teams to staging.

Whether the new class would hold in the semifinal, she could not say; ninety minutes was not enough to be sure of anything. But when the volunteers waved their team forward, Makayla closed the laptop, picked up the robot, and carried it toward the field with the test's green bar still bright in her mind.

story:
The living room of Grandma Ruth's house had a bay window and a rug with a pattern of faded roses, and Paige had decided it was a theater. She moved the coffee table to the hall, pushed the armchair against the wall, and marked the audience's edge with a length of blue painter's tape, third strip from the roll because the first two had curled. Her cousin Theo stood at the tape line holding the script of the one-act, a twelve-page thing Paige had written over the summer about two brothers arguing over a toolbox.

"We start blocking today," she said. "That means I decide where you move."

"You mean we don't just stand there."

"You can't just stand there. It looks dead." She said it more sharply than she meant to, and Theo raised his eyebrows, which was his way of impugning her authority without saying a word out loud. Their neighbor Marcus, who was playing the older brother, was already on the rug, reading his lines in the low voice he used when he thought something was beneath him.

They ran the first scene. Marcus circled the toolbox, then crossed the rug toward the window, and Theo, following his cue, stepped to meet him, and Paige stopped them. From the armchair where she sat, her view of Theo was gone. Marcus's shoulder and part of his jacket covered him entirely. She walked to the tape line, crouched, stood, walked to the other side of the rug, crouched again. Theo was still missing.

"Marcus, hold. Theo, you disappeared."

"I'm right here."

"I know you're right here. The audience can't see you." She went back to the armchair and they ran it again, and again Theo vanished behind Marcus's body, and Marcus got to the end of his speech, a long peroration about their dead father and the ethics of keeping things that were never yours, and Paige stopped the run a second time. Marcus complained that she kept interrupting his momentum. She said momentum didn't matter if half the scene was invisible. He called her bellicose, in the joking way he used words he'd learned for the SAT, and she let it go because she was busy staring at the floor.

There was a natural place to fix it, she thought. Marcus crossed, so something had to answer the crossing, a shift, a small movement the other way, the way the rose rug balanced its own pattern, dark on one end and dark on the other. She didn't have a word for it. She drew the rug on the back of the script, drew an arrow for Marcus's path, then a smaller arrow for Theo, curved, opening away from Marcus's shoulder.

"Theo, when he crosses, you drift downstage. Not toward him. Slightly away, angled, so the two of you split the space."

"Like magnets."

"Opposite, sort of. Just try it."

They ran the scene a third time. Marcus crossed toward the window, Theo eased down and to the left, and from the armchair Paige could see both of them, whole bodies, both faces. It looked, suddenly, composed. She felt something loosen in her chest but kept her voice flat. "Again," she said, "from the top of the page," and they did it four more times until the adjustment stopped looking like an adjustment and started looking like nothing at all, which she understood was the point.

That evening Grandma Ruth brought out iced tea and stayed to watch a full run. She had acted in community theater for thirty years, and Paige kept bracing for a critique, but Grandma said nothing until the end, when Theo, drifting downstage on Marcus's cross, found his new mark and settled into it.

"That's called countering," Grandma said, setting down her glass.

"Countering," Paige repeated.

"When one actor crosses and the other shifts position to balance the stage, that's countering. Both of them stay visible to the audience." She said it the way she said things about her garden, plainly, and then she asked whether they wanted more tea.

Paige sat with her glass and thought about how she'd gotten there, half by drawing arrows and half by accident, and about whether the composed look she'd seen was something she had made or something the room had given her. She couldn't decide, and she wasn't sure it mattered, and she wasn't sure it didn't.

On Saturday she taped out the stage again and pulled the armchair to its corner, and stood at the tape line with the script rolled in her hand. "Places," she said. "Top of the play."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
story:
Nolan had taped his poster to the folding table at 7:40 in the morning, and by 8:15 the bottom right corner had already curled up like it wanted to leave. The poster said, in letters he had traced twice with marker because the first attempt was crooked, HOW HEAT MOVES A REACTION AT EQUILIBRIUM. Below it stood his whole project: three beakers of cobalt chloride solution in a warm water bath, an ice bath, and a torpid puddle of room-temperature nothing that had so far refused to change color at all.

"You spelled Chatelier wrong," said Priya from the next table, leaning over a volcano that her little brother had technically built. She was a senior too, waiting for her own judging slot in the physics row, and she had been harassing him since they unloaded the bus. "It's C-h-a-t-e-l-i-e-r. You wrote Chatiler. Twice."

Nolan crouched and looked. He had written Chatiler twice, in the careful hand of someone who had been very sure of himself. "That's how you say it," he said, which was not the same as how you spell it, and they both knew it. He peeled off the misspelled labels and relettered them on the backs of judging sheets, his hands smelling of marker and cold water from the ice bath.

The judge arrived at nine. She was young, badge crooked, and she did what every judge did at every fair Nolan had ever attended: she looked at the beakers before she looked at him. The hot one had gone blue. The iced one had gone pink, a pink so assertive it almost glowed. "So explain what I'm seeing," she said.

"When a reaction's at equilibrium, it's balanced, forward and backward happening at the same rate," Nolan said, and moved the iced beaker into the warm bath to show her the pink fading, the blue creeping back through it like weather. "If you change the temperature, the balance shifts. Cooling it pushes it one way, heating it pushes it the other. The system answers the change by partly undoing it." He had a paragraph memorized about this and he delivered about half of it before he noticed she was frowning at his poster.

"Who figured that out?" she asked.

Nolan opened his mouth and then, honestly, closed it. He had written the principle down from a textbook three weeks ago, practiced the demonstration until he could do it half asleep, and never once asked whose idea it was. "It's called Le Chatelier's principle," he said, pointing at his freshly corrected sign, which now, mercifully, spelled it right. "That's all I've got."

Priya, who had drifted over with her brother's volcano still smoking faintly at her elbow, said, "You named your entire project after a man you can't identify. That's like writing a fan letter to an address."

The fair was held in the front hall of the science museum, which Nolan had walked through twice without seeing, because when you are carrying three beakers and a hot plate you see only doorways. Now he walked it properly, past a case of pinned butterflies whose genus labels had beguiled him as a kid, past the pendulum, until he found the chemistry wall: a long panel about equilibrium with a portrait of a bearded man in a high collar. The caption underneath said that the principle was named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884. Nolan read it twice, then took a picture of it with his phone, then felt slightly embarrassed about taking a picture of a museum caption, as though it were a celebrity.

"He's French," Nolan reported when he got back. "Stated it in 1884. Henry Louis Le Chatelier." He held up the phone. Priya examined the portrait with the severity of someone appraising a rival. "He looks like he never once spilled anything," she said. "I don't trust him."

The judge came back around at eleven, during the second round, and stood at Nolan's table while he ran the demonstration again, this time narrating it differently. "So the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier stated this in 1884," he said, mostly to hear whether it sounded natural. "Nobody taught the system to do this. It just does it. You push, it leans back." He lifted the blue beaker out of the heat and set it in the ice, and they both watched the pink climb up through it from the bottom, slow as sunrise in a jar.

"It's tidy," the judge said. "Do you think it always works? Every reaction?"

And here Nolan stopped, because he had a poster that implied yes and a brain that suspected no. "I don't know," he said. "Mine shifts clean. The textbook says temperature changes shift equilibrium. But I only ran one reaction, and I got the man's name wrong for three weeks, so I'm not going to pretend I ran the universe." The judge wrote something on her clipboard that he could not read upside down, and Priya, from the next table, mouthed the word show-off, which from her was practically a ribbon.

When the awards were posted on the gym door at two o'clock, Nolan's name was third in chemistry, behind a girl who had grown crystals in a fish tank and ahead of nobody, because there were only three entries. He took the red third-place card back to his table, propped it against the middle beaker, which had finally committed to a violet sort of shrug, neither pink nor blue, warm nor cold, exactly balanced between the two baths.

"There he is," Priya said, tapping the portrait still open on Nolan's phone. "Say thank you."

"Merci," Nolan told the bearded man, and turned the phone face-down on the table.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
story:
Morgan spread the current map across a flat slab of limestone at the quarry's edge, weighting the corners with four chunks of slate so the wind off the water couldn't take it. The map showed the Atlantic in arrows and colors, the Gulf Stream a warm red ribbon unspooling from Florida toward Norway, and she was supposed to stand up in front of her freshman seminar on Thursday and explain, in eight minutes, how that ribbon kept Europe from freezing. She had written the script already. The script was wrong.

That was the trouble, and she had known it was the trouble since Tuesday, when Priya had leaned across the library table with her laptop turned around and said, "You're going to want to see this, but you're not going to want to see this." Priya, ebullient even when delivering bad news, had found a study from 2002, led by a man named Richard Seager, and its argument was that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters. Not a small correction. An amputation.

"I'll just do both," Morgan had said at the library. "The old story and the new one."

"That's not a position," Priya said. "That's a buffet."

Now, at the quarry, Morgan read the printout again by the light reflected off the green water. The stone walls around her dropped forty feet, striated and pale, an old working cut gone lazy and full of rain. She'd been coming here since she was nine, when her father would lift her over the chain and say the water was deeper than her whole future. He liked a line like that. He was a lawyer, the kind who could hold forth on the jurisprudence of trespass at length, and he'd offered that lecture on the drive out this morning while she held the map rolled on her knees like a baton. She'd said yes, sure, she'd be careful, and mostly she'd been thinking about Seager.

The fact was she'd loved the old story. A warm river crossing an ocean to hold a continent's winters open, that was a story with a hero in it. Seager's version had no hero, just prevailing winds doing their quiet work and the ocean taking in heat all summer and letting it go slowly, like a stone that stays warm after sunset. She'd spent an hour the night before trying to find some way both could be true at once, some generous arithmetic, and had gotten nowhere except a page of crossed-out paragraphs.

Her phone buzzed against the limestone. A message from Priya, and Morgan could hear the grin in it before she'd finished reading. "Dear Morgan, breaker of hearts, inventor of buffets. My grandmother wants to know if you're coming to dinner Sunday. Also I found the actual paper, not just the summary, and it's worse for you than you think, it's very persuasive. Also also, your hero the Gulf Stream is still real and still warm, nobody's taking your ribbon away, they're just making it share. Bring the map Sunday. Bring sunscreen. Bring an argument, not a shrug. Yours in turmoil, Priya." Morgan laughed once, out loud, alone, the sound bouncing off the quarry wall and coming back smaller.

She stripped off her sneakers and waded in to her shins, map behind her on the rock, and stood looking at the far wall while the cold climbed her calves. The water here stored the sun the same way the paper said the ocean did, she supposed, and then caught herself doing it, converting everything into evidence. Still, she let the thought stand. Her father had once explained that a good argument doesn't hide the cases it loses, it absorbs them, and that the law was mostly this, not a set of verdicts but a record of what survived. She'd rolled her eyes at fifteen. She could admit now, at eighteen, standing in a quarry, that the idea might underwrite what she said on Thursday.

So she would say it like this: the Gulf Stream carries real warmth north, and that part of the old story holds. But the study argued that winds and the ocean's seasonal heat storage, more than the Gulf Stream itself, explained most of Europe's mild winters, and she could not make that sentence go away, so she would hand it to the seminar whole. What she couldn't yet say was how much of the mildness belonged to each part, whether anyone could say that at all, and she would end her eight minutes on that open question and stand there while her classmates looked at her.

She waded back out, dripping, and knelt over the map. With the red pen she wrote in the margin, in letters big enough to read from a podium, "most of it, not all of it, and the rest is a question." Then she folded the printout into her back pocket, gathered her four slates, and climbed the trail toward the chain and the road, phone already buzzing again in her hand.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
story:
The article was four paragraphs long, in German, and Levi had promised his study partner he would read it aloud by four o'clock. He had chosen it from a news site because it was short, and only after printing it did he notice how strange it looked on the page. Words were capitalized everywhere, not just at the beginnings of sentences. The Finanzminister had resigned. There were questions about Euro and Steuer and Milliarde. He set the printout on the table beside the dictionary and counted, in the first paragraph alone, eleven capital letters that were not starting sentences.

Priya arrived at five past four with two granola bars and put one on his side of the table. "You have twenty minutes before I have to meet my sister," she said. "Go."

He read the first sentence and stopped. The dictionary work he had done that morning had prepared him for the vocabulary, roughly, but not for the way the capitals scattered themselves through every line. He pointed at the page. "Why are all these words capitalized? Steuer, Milliarde, Untersuchung. It's not just names. Look, it's everywhere."

Priya leaned over. She had taken a semester of German before switching to Spanish, and she squinted at the article for a moment. "German capitalizes every noun," she said. "Not just names. Every single one." She tapped the page. "Everything with a capital in there is a noun."

Levi sat back. He read the second sentence again with that in mind and found that it worked like a diagram lying flat on the page. The verbs stayed lowercase and the nouns rose up out of the line, and even where he did not know a word, he could see at a glance what job it was doing. He put his finger under a capitalized word he had not looked up, Haushalt, and guessed from its position that it was a thing, an object of some kind, probably the budget the article kept circling around. He checked the dictionary. Budget. He had guessed it without the translation, from the shape of the sentence alone.

But the reading was not going to be only a matter of shape. He tried the second paragraph aloud, and it was about the scandal itself: the minister's aide had absconded with money from a regional development fund, according to prosecutors, and was believed to be in Zurich. Levi stumbled through the clause twice, and Priya corrected his pronunciation of the word for money, which he had been saying with an English vowel. Then the article turned to the politics. A regional parliament was threatening a plebiscite on the whole development program if the investigation was not made public, and one opposition figure was quoted calling the government's response bellicose, which Levi at first misread as a place name because it was capitalized. He stared at it, confused, until he remembered that it could not be a noun if it mattered where it sat; it was modifying something, and he looked it up and found it meant aggressive, hostile to discussion. He said the line aloud a second time and heard how the quotation worked as an accusation.

"Okay," Priya said. "Now the summary. In English, just the main points, like you'd tell someone at dinner."

Levi put the article face down. He started with the resignation, then the aide and the fund, then the threatened vote. He got through two sentences and stopped, because he realized he did not know, from the article, whether the plebiscite was a serious threat or theater for the cameras, and the difference seemed to matter if he was going to summarize it honestly. The article treated it as leverage; the opposition figure treated it as inevitable. He said so out loud. "I can say they're threatening a vote, but I can't actually tell you whether it'll happen. The article doesn't decide."

"So say that part too," Priya said. "That's allowed."

He started over, slower, and this time he kept the uncertainty inside the summary instead of smoothing it out. He said the aide had fled with the money and had not been found, that the minister had resigned without admitting anything, that a public vote was being threatened and that the article did not say whether the threat would hold. When he finished, Priya took the last bite of her granola bar and looked at the clock. She said his second attempt was better than his first, and he said the capitals had helped more than the dictionary had, which was a thing he had not expected to say about a language.

"You have the same article for Friday," she said, gathering her bag. "Read it once for the nouns and once for everything else."

Levi turned the paper over and looked at the third paragraph, where the words rose out of their lines like stones in shallow water, and put his pen on the first one he did not yet know.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
story:
Thomas had three sticky notes, one pink, one blue, one yellow, and a photocopied page of Mozart's Piano Sonata in F, K. 332, second movement, spread across his knees in the last row of the concert hall. His music theory teacher, Ms. Achterberg, had offered extra credit to anyone who could codify the movement's structure by Monday, marking where each section began. Thomas wanted the credit, but more than that he wanted to stop feeling like a fraud in that class, the boy who played trumpet well enough and understood nothing. He had decided the way to understand was to hear it live, so he had spent his lawn-mowing money on a cheap ticket and arrived forty minutes early, when the hall was nearly empty and the piano tuner was still picking at a string.

He laid the pink note at the top of the page. That part seemed safe. The opening bars were obviously a beginning, the place where the themes were presented, the first thing the ear met. The blue and yellow were harder. He slid the blue note down to the double bar halfway through the page, where the melody shifted into something minor and restless, then moved it again, then moved it back. He had read the textbook's account so many times the sentence had worn smooth in his memory, and he recited it under his breath like a charm: the exposition presents the themes, the development works them through other keys, and the recapitulation brings them back.

An old man settled into the seat beside him, shaking rain off a folded newspaper. "You're the only person under sixty here," he said. "And you've brought homework."

"Sort of," Thomas said. "I'm trying to mark the form. Sonata form. It's got three sections."

"Ah," the man said. He tucked the newspaper under his arm and said nothing more, which Thomas found almost worse than interruption.

When the pianist walked out, Thomas arranged his three notes along the top edge of the score like flags on a contested border. The hall lights dimmed. The first movement passed over him in a blur of admiration he couldn't analyze, and then the Adagio began, and he bent so close to the page that his breath moved the pink note.

For a while it went as he had planned. The opening theme arrived, then a second, sweeter one, and Thomas felt a small, ridiculous pride, as if he had written them. Then the music began to wander. Keys dissolved and reformed; the theme he thought he knew turned up in a register he didn't expect, bent into shapes he couldn't find on his photocopied page at all. He moved the blue note three times during the development alone. His pencil hovered, uncertain. In biology last semester he had liked immunology precisely because everything had a mechanism, a cascade, a reason each cell did what it did, and he kept wanting music to behave the same way, to be a system he could memorize. It refused. It drifted, and he drifted with it, and slowly he stopped trying to mark every measure and just listened.

Then it happened. The opening theme returned, whole, at peace, in the key where it had started, and Thomas's stomach dropped because the yellow note was in the wrong place, stuck a dozen bars too early. He had mistaken a brief pause for a return, a resting for a resolution. The real recapitulation was happening now, unmistakable, and he peeled the yellow note off the page and pressed it down where the melody truly came back. Beside him the old man glanced over and saw the note move.

"You found it," the man whispered.

"I put it wrong first," Thomas whispered back, half apologetic.

"Everybody puts it wrong first." The man turned back to the music, and Thomas, his ears still hot, found that this was somehow the most encouraging thing anyone had said to him all year.

Afterwards, in the lobby, with the crowd thinning toward the doors, Thomas spread the score on a windowsill and looked at his three notes. Pink at the beginning, blue where the wandering started, yellow where the theme came home. He could see the shape of the whole movement now, laid out in color, and yet he knew the blue note was still approximate, that somewhere in that middle section he had guessed, and that his guess would probably cost him a point or two on Monday. He took out his pencil and wrote a small question mark beside it, deciding he would ask Ms. Achterberg not for the answer but for a way to check it himself, some trick of the ear for hearing when a key has truly changed. The old man passed on his way out, nodded at the score, and said, "Same seats next month?" Thomas looked up, and the rain on the glass behind him had turned to a bright, thin drizzle. "I'll be here," he said.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
story:
William had failed the projectile quiz on Tuesday, and by Saturday he was at the playground with his textbook, a calculator, and a basketball he had brought mostly out of spite. The quiz had asked where a ball would land, and he had guessed, because the numbers in his notes swam together into a single anxious blur. His friend Ada had texted him a single line that morning: swing sets, 3 o'clock, bring your sorry grade.

She was already there, sitting cross-legged on the mulch under the monkey bars with her own book open. She did not look up when he dropped his bag beside her. "You look blase about failing," she said, meaning his shrug, his slow amble, the way he let the basketball roll out of his hand and bump against the slide.

"I'm not blase. I'm conserving energy."

"Uh-huh." She flipped to a page, and he saw his own handwriting in the margin, a small desperate question mark. "Okay. Tell me what you remember."

"Gravity pulls down. The ball goes forward. Something about angles."

"That's it? That's what you wrote for a whole quiz?" She lobbed a pinecone at him, and he caught it without thinking, and then he looked at his hand as though it had acted without permission. "Throw it back," she said. "Overhand, kind of flat."

He threw it. It sailed over the mulch in a shallow arc and landed near the tire swing. Ada watched it the whole way. "Your arm knows more physics than your brain does," she said. "Same speed forward the entire flight. Gravity only messes with up and down. Those are two separate things happening at once."

William sat down on the mulch. He was quiet long enough that a jogger passed the fence, long enough for a toddler at the sand pit to fill and empty a red bucket twice. "Separate," he repeated. He drew it, an arrow going sideways and an arrow going straight down, then a curve connecting where the pinecone had started to where it had landed. "So if I figure out how long it's in the air..."

"Then you know how far it goes," Ada said. "Horizontal distance is just the constant horizontal velocity multiplied by the time in the air."

He copied the sentence exactly, underlined it, and then, because underlining felt like something his September self would do to feel productive, he tested it. He took the basketball to the end of the mulched area, walked off ten paces, and threw the ball flat and hard, counting under his breath. One, two, one-halves. It bounced once on the packed dirt near the fence.

"That's one second," Ada called. "Roughly."

"Roughly one second, roughly ten paces." He went back, threw again with the same arm, the same flick of the wrist, and got roughly the same bounce. The ball did not care that he had failed a quiz. It went the same distance every time because it was doing what it did, not what he felt about it.

They sat with the numbers after that. Ada wrote a time on her palm in pen, and William found the horizontal speed in his notes, and he multiplied, and the answer came out to a distance, and he checked it against the answer key in the back of the book, and it matched. He laughed once, short, surprised. "That's all it is? You find the time first, and then one multiplication gives you the landing point?"

"That's all it is. Ignoring air resistance, which we always do, which is a lie, but a useful lie."

He thought about that. He threw the pinecone again, flatter, with more pace, and this time it landed short of where he expected, and he could not tell whether his throw had changed or the wind had or whether his counting had drifted. The book gave him a world with no air, and the playground gave him one with air, and both of them were true enough to be worth knowing. He wrote a second line under the first: the numbers work if you hold the world still.

"It's like bio," Ada said, gathering her pens. "We spent all week on parasitism, one thing living off another, and I kept thinking the chapter was lying too, because tapeworms don't sit politely in their hosts the way the diagram shows."

"You're saying physics and tapeworms have the same problem."

"I'm saying diagrams are always cleaner than playgrounds."

The afternoon was thinning. The toddler had gone, and the swing set chains hung still, and William stood at his ten paces with the ball one more time. He counted the throw, watched the bounce, marked the landing spot with the heel of his shoe in the dirt.

"One and a half seconds," he said. "So it went one and a half times farther than the first one." He dragged his heel sideways, measuring it out. "Now I beseech you, tell me the quiz on Monday is exactly this."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
story:
Ethan spread the ocean current map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with his sister's smoothest skipping stones, four of them borrowed from the coffee can by the back door. The map had come folded in the packet from the summer program at the marine science institute, along with a letter that said, in the friendliest possible font, that all incoming students should arrive able to explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. He had eleven days. He had also, according to his sister Dee, promised to help her build the thing she was currently dragging across the lawn.

The thing was a rabbit hutch, or the idea of one, a lean-to of pallet wood and zip ties that Dee, who was thirteen and had been saving for a rabbit since March, intended to finish before their mother changed her mind about the rabbit entirely. She dropped her end of a board in the grass and came to stand over the map, casting a shadow across the North Atlantic.

"What is that, the ocean?"

"Currents," Ethan said. "The red parts move warm water north, the blue parts move cold water south." He traced the wide red ribbon that peeled off the American coast and aimed itself toward Europe like a thrown rope. What he could not yet do, and what the letter implied he should be able to do, was say why that ribbon made London rainy and green instead of frozen like Labrador, which sat at the same latitude and was, on the map, ice.

"I want the hutch done before Saturday," Dee said. "That's my want, and I'm stating it out loud so you can't say you didn't know."

"Tonight," he said. "After I figure this out."

She went back to her boards, and he bent over the map with his phone, because the packet's reading was dense and he hoped for something a person could actually picture. What he found instead was a story, and the story was better than the reading. Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769. Franklin, who had crossed the Atlantic multiple times and never once thought to wonder why some voyages dragged, got the crucial knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain. The captains had known for years. They rode the current going east and dodged it coming home, saving days, while the British packet ships plowed straight through it and lost those days, their masters complaining about fogs and delays and never once connecting the complaints to the warm water under their keels. There were no satellites. There was a whaler who watched the water, told his cousin, and the cousin had it printed.

Ethan sat back on the bench. What snagged him was not the physics of the current, which he could more or less parrot, but the shape of the discovery: the people who knew the thing best were the ones nobody thought to ask. He thought about his own essay for the program, which he had titled, with a seventeen-year-old's confidence, "The Utility of Ocean Circulation," a title chosen mostly because he had recently learned the word utilitarianism in ethics class and liked the sound of applying it to water. Utilitarianism said you judged an action by its consequences, by the days saved, and the captains had been quietly consequentialist for a century before anyone charted what they knew. He also suspected, sitting there, that his essay was worse than Dee's hutch, which at least existed.

"That is the most boring thing you've ever looked at," Dee said, hammering something. "Your face is doing the concentrating face."

"There were whalers," Ethan said, "who knew the ocean better than the scientists, and nobody asked them for a hundred years."

"So ask somebody," she said, with the brutality of thirteen.

He looked at the map again, then at the fence, then at the gray sky that had begun, in a way that did not portend anything good for the hutch, to thicken over the neighbor's poplar. He thought about his grandfather, who had driven trucks for forty years and who claimed he could tell you the best route to Tulsa in any weather, and about how nobody in the family had ever once written it down. Then he did what he should have done an hour ago, which was to read the map the way Folger would have, as a driver reads a road: not as an explanation but as a set of lanes. Warm lane going east, cold lane coming back. The warm lane delivered its heat to the boreal edge of Europe, to places that by all rights should have been tundra and were instead mild and damp, and that was the sentence he would say in September, plain, no essay title required. He could say it now. He tried it out loud to the yard: "Warm water moves north across the Atlantic and releases its heat near Europe, so northern Europe stays warmer than other places at the same latitude." It sounded almost too simple, and he trusted it more for that, though he still could not have said exactly why the water moved, and he was honest enough with himself to note the gap rather than paper over it.

The first drops hit the map and he lunged for the stones, and Dee was already shouting about the hutch, and they carried the boards two at a time under the porch roof while the rain came down through the poplar in long silver ropes. They worked until dark, Ethan holding, Dee hammering, the map drying in a safe curl on the porch swing.

"Say the ocean thing again," Dee said, driving a nail. "The whaler part."

"My cousin is a whaler," Ethan said, in his best old-timey voice, "and he says you're sailing against a river in the sea."

Dee laughed so hard she bent the nail.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
Brody had claimed the living room for the weekend because the school stage was booked for the jazz band, and the one-act he was directing opened in eleven days. His mother had moved the coffee table against the wall without being asked, which he took as a kind of blessing. On the carpet he had laid out the stage with painter's tape, a rectangle roughly to scale, and inside it he arranged two kitchen chairs, a footstool, and the long sofa from the den to stand in for the set.

The play was a two-hander about brothers dividing their dead father's tools, twelve pages that had enraptured Brody the first time he read it, though he could not have said exactly why. Something about how little the brothers said while handing each other wrenches. He had assumed directing would mean deciding what the lines meant and telling the actors. He was learning, slowly, that it mostly meant deciding where people stood.

Priya and Marcus arrived at ten with bags of chips and a printed script Priya had already annotated in three colors. They ran the first scene in the taped rectangle, and almost immediately the sofa began to travel. Marcus dragged it forward to sit on it, then Priya angled it while crossing to the window, and by the fourth run-through it had migrated nearly two feet from where it started, drifting toward the edge of the taped stage like a slow barge. "You're losing your light," Brody kept saying, although there was no light in the living room, only the lamp his mother kept switching on in the hallway.

He tried the polite version of authority, asking whether they might reset between runs. Marcus, who was garrulous even for someone playing a taciturn brother, narrated each reset like a golf announcer, and Priya reset with theatrical sighs. The sofa crept anyway. It crept because actors, Brody realized, watch each other rather than the floor, and each of them nudged the furniture a little to clear a path, and none of the nudges agreed. He sat on the arm of the couch with his chin in his hand and wondered whether professional directors had this problem or whether it was only him, only this room, only a footstool standing in for a workbench.

He remembered then the floor of the real stage at school, how it had looked after the fall musical struck. There had been little Xs of colored tape everywhere, orange and green and yellow, leftovers from some earlier production, and he had assumed they were garbage. On Monday he went in early, found the tape still there, and peeled up a green X to examine it. It was stiff, matte, thinner than duct tape, and when he pressed it back down his thumbnail left no residue on the pad of his thumb. In the drama room's supply cabinet, on a shelf between gaff rolls, he found a roll labeled the same way, and a label is not an explanation, but it was a start.

"That's spike tape," said Jules, the senior who ran the light board and was, as far as Brody could tell, always in the building. She was coiling cable and did not look up. "It marks where furniture and actors go on the stage floor." Brody asked if it came in colors, and she said all of them, and that was the whole conversation, which he appreciated.

He took the roll home. That evening, before Priya and Marcus arrived, he tore short strips and laid them at each corner of the sofa, a small bright X at every leg, and one on the carpet where Marcus sat, and one where Priya had to end her cross to the window. When the actors came in, Priya looked at the tape and said it looked like a crime scene, but she stood on her mark.

The strange thing was how little he had to say after that. The sofa stopped wandering. Every time it drifted a few inches, somebody glanced down, saw the tape, and pulled it back, and the correction became part of the action, so that Marcus's character now hauled the couch into place as though it were a stubborn thing his father had owned, which in the play it was. Priya found a moment where she toed her mark before speaking, a little hesitation, like someone checking that the floor would hold her. Brody had not asked for any of it. He wrote in his notebook, where he was keeping a running list of things he did not understand about directing, that the tape had given him back about ten minutes of every rehearsal, and that those minutes had somehow become the best part.

He did not fully believe his own note. It was possible the tape was a fix and the moments were accidents, and it was possible the moments were the point and the tape only a trick, and he could not yet tell those apart. In math class they had been proving things all year, and his teacher kept insisting that every theorem rests on a smaller statement, a lemma, something you prove first so the big thing follows. Brody thought the sofa's position might be the lemma of his whole production, the small settled thing that made everything after it possible to argue. Or the metaphor might be wrong. He put a question mark next to it.

The night before they moved to the real stage, Priya and Marcus ran the entire twelve pages without stopping, and the sofa did not travel an inch. At the last line, Marcus picked up the footstool and set it down on one of the green Xs with a small deliberate bang, and Priya laughed the way people laugh when something is true. Brody stayed in his chair after they gathered their bags, looking at the little field of tape on the carpet, the Xs glowing faintly under the lamp. On Sunday, before his mother reclaimed the room, he knelt and peeled up each strip, one by one, and pressed them onto the inside back cover of his notebook, where they stuck and held.
